## NUR AL-DIN ALI AND THE MAIDEN ANIS AL-JALIS

Shahrazad said:—I have heard, O fortunate King of deep intelligence, that among the Kings of Bassorah there was a King who loved the poor and needy and cared for his subjects. He gave his wealth to all who believed in Mohammed (whom Allah bless and save!), and he was just as one of the poets described him:—

->A King who, when enemy hosts invade, ❈ Receives them with lance-thrusts and sword-swings;<-
->He writes his name on chests in thin red lines, ❈ And scatters the cavalry in wild confusion.<-

---

¹ In addition to note 2, p. 2, and note 2, p. 14, vol. 1, I may add that “Shahrázád,” in the *Shams al-Loghat* <note>The Sun of Languages</note>, is the proper name of a King. L. Langlès (*The Voyages of Sinbad the Sailor and the Deception of Women* <note>original: "Les Voyages de Sindibâd Le Marin et La Ruse des Femmes"</note>, first added to Savary’s Grammar and reprinted 1814) explains it as “the cypress, the beauty of the city”; and he is followed by Kazimirski (*Enis el-Djelis*, Paris, 1847). Ouseley (*Oriental Collections*) makes Shahrazad = town-born; and others see it as an Arabic form of *Chehr-azad* (“free of face” or “noble of countenance”), the nickname <note>original: "petit nom"</note> of Queen Humay, for whom see the final Essay. The name of the sister—whom the *Fihrist* <note>The Index</note> turns into a *Kahramanah*, or nurse, commonly written Dunyazad—would mean “child of gold pieces,” “freed by gold pieces,” or “one who has no need of gold pieces”: *Din-zad* = child of faith; and *Daynazad*, proposed by Langlès, “free from debt (!)” I have adopted Macnaghten’s Dunyazad. “Shahryar,” which Scott horribly writes “Shier-ear,” is translated by the *Shams* as “King of the world,” “absolute monarch,” and “the court of Anushirwan,” while the *Burhan-i-Qati* <note>The Decisive Proof</note> defines it as a King of Kings and the proper name of a town. Shahr-baz is also the name of a town in Samarkand.

² Arabic “Malik,” used here as in our storybooks: “Pompey was a wise and powerful King,” says the *Gesta Romanorum* <note>The Deeds of the Romans</note>. This King is, as will appear, a Regent or Governor under Harun al-Rashid. In the next tale, he is the Viceroy of Damascus, where he is also called “Sultan.”

³ The Bulaq Edition gives the lines as follows:—

->The spear was his pen, and the hearts of his enemies ❈ His paper, and he dipped it in blood for ink;<-
->Therefore our ancestors called the spear *Khattiyah*, ❈ Meaning, I think, that one shall write with it.<-

The pun is in “Khattiyah,” which can mean a female writer and also a spear, from Khatt-Hajar, a region in the province of Al-Bahrayn (Persian Gulf) and Oman. This is where the best Indian bamboos were landed and fashioned into lances. Imr al-Kays (*Mu’allakah* v. 4.) sings of “our dark spears firmly made of Khattiyan cane”; Al-Busiri of “the brown lances of Khatt”; see also Lebid v. 50 and *Hamasah* pp. 26, 231: Antar mentions the “Spears of Khatt” and “Rudaynian lances.” Rudaynah is said to have been the...

His name was King Mohammed bin Sulayman al-Zayni, and he had two Viziers: one named Al-Mu’ín, son of Sáwí, and the other Al-Fazl, son of Khákán. Al-Fazl was the most generous man of his age and lived an upright life, so that everyone loved him and the wise flocked to him for counsel. His subjects used to pray for his long life because he embodied the very best qualities—encouraging goodness and kindness while preventing evil and mischief. But the Vizier Mu’in bin Sawi, on the contrary, hated people <gloss>1</gloss> and did not love what was good. He was made of nothing but ill-will, just as was said of him:—

> Stick with the noble, sons of the noble! It is always Nature's test *
> That nobles born of nobles shall excel in noble deeds.
> Avoid the small-souled and meanly bred, for it is the law *
> That mean deeds come from men of mean blood and breeding.

As much as the people loved and adored Al-Fazl bin Khakan, they utterly hated the mean and miserly Mu’in bin Sawi. It happened one day, by the decree of Fate, that King Mohammed bin Sulayman al-Zayni sat on his throne with his officers of state around him. He summoned his Vizier Al-Fazl and said to him, “I wish to have a slave-girl of extraordinary beauty—perfect in her charms, exquisite in her proportions, and gifted with every virtue.” The courtiers said, “Such a girl cannot be bought for less than ten thousand gold pieces.” Upon hearing this, the Sultan called for his treasurer and said, “Take ten thousand dinars <term>gold coins</term> to the house of Al-Fazl bin Khakan.” The treasurer did the King’s bidding. The Minister then departed, having received the royal command to visit the slave market every day and hire brokers for this task. Moreover, the King issued orders that no girls worth more than a thousand gold pieces should be bought or sold without first being shown to the Vizier. Consequently, no broker purchased a slave-girl before she had been presented to the Minister; but none pleased him, until one day a

---

...wife of one Samhár, who was as famous for lances as the city of Ferrara was for swords <note>Ferrara, Italy, was renowned for its high-quality sword blades</note>; others claim she was the wife of Al-Ka'azab and believe Samhár to be a town in Abyssinia where the best weapons were manufactured. The pen is the <term>Calamus</term> <note>original: "Calamus," Latin for reed/pen</note> or *Kalam* (a reed cut for a pen), of which the finest and hardest are brought from Java; they require the least sharpening. The rhetorical device in the text is called *Husn al-Ta'alíl*, or etiology <note>assigning a poetic cause to a natural fact</note>; it is as admirable to the Arabs as it seems trivial to us.

The broker came to the house and found the Vizier mounting his horse, intending to go to the palace. So he caught hold of his stirrup and said:

> O you, who give a sweet flavor to the royal state, ❧ You are a Vizier who shall never lose favor!
> You have restored dead Generosity to life for men; ❧ May such high efforts never lack God’s grace!

Then he said, “O my lord, that extraordinary object for whom the royal command was issued has at last been found;” <note>The original sentence is written in a very ornate, flowery style.</note> and the Vizier replied, “Bring her here to me!” So the broker went away and returned after a short while, bringing a young woman dressed in the richest clothing. She was a maiden as straight as a spear and five feet tall, with a developing bosom and large eyes as black as if they were lined with kohl <term>a traditional dark eyeliner powder</term>. Her dewy lips were sweeter than syrup or the sherbet one sips. She was a smooth-cheeked and shapely-faced young girl, whose slender waist was complemented by full hips. Her form was more pleasing than a branch waving at the top of a tree, and her voice was softer and gentler than the morning breeze, just as one of those who described her said:

> A strange charm adorns her brows, which shine like the moon's disk; ❧ Oh, she is sweeter to the taste than the finest syrup <note>original: "Robb," a fruit syrup or "rob."</note> or raisins from the vine.
> The highest heaven <term>the Empyrean</term> keeps a throne for her in a high and glorious state, ❧ For her wit and wisdom, her slender form, and her graceful silhouette.
> In the "heaven" of her face, she displays the seven stars <note>original: "seven-fold stars," referring to the Septentriones or the Big Dipper.</note>, ❧ Which guard her cheeks like satellites against any spy’s gaze.
> If a man should cast a secret glance or steal a look at her from afar, ❧ His heart is struck by lightning bolts shot from those piercing eyes.

When the Vizier saw her, she filled him with immense admiration. Perfectly pleased, he turned to the broker and asked, “What is the price of this girl?” The broker answered, “Her market value is ten thousand dinars <term>gold coins</term>. However, her owner swears that this sum will not even cover the cost of the chickens she has eaten, the wine she has drunk, and the robes of honor given to her teacher. She has learned calligraphy, grammar, and linguistics; the commentaries on the Quran; the principles of law and religion; the rules of medicine; the calendar; and the art of playing musical instruments.” <note>This list of accomplishments is humorously extensive, much like a traditional list of "proper" Victorian feminine accomplishments.</note> The Vizier said, “Bring me her master.” So the broker brought him at once and,

And behold, he was a Persian of whom there was left only what the years had spared; for he was as bald and scabby as a vulture, and like a wall trembling on the verge of collapse. Time had battered him with painful blows, yet he was not willing to depart from this world; just as the poet said:

> Time has shattered my entire frame, * Oh! how time has shattered me.
> Time, with its royal power, can tame * Manly strength and vigorous energy.
> There was a time in my youth when none * Traveled more swiftly or fast:
> Now time remains but my strength is gone, * Youth is finished, and my speed is past. <note>The eight-line stanza occurs in Night 15. I quote Torrens (p. 360) for variety.</note>

The Wazir asked him, “Are you content to sell this slave-girl to the Sultan for ten thousand dinars <term>gold coins</term>?” and the Persian answered, “By Allah, if I offered her to the King for nothing, it would only be my duty.” <note>A polite way of accepting the offer.</note> So the Minister ordered the money to be brought and watched as it was weighed out for the Persian. The merchant then stood before him and said, “With our lord the Wazir’s permission, I have something to say;” and the Wazir replied, “Speak whatever is on your mind!” 

“It is my opinion,” continued the slave-dealer, “that you should not take the girl to the King today; for she has just finished a journey; the change of climate <note>original: "water and air." To express our “change of climate,” Easterners say, “change of water and air,” putting water first.</note> has affected her, and the exhaustion of travel has worn her down. Instead, keep her quietly in your palace for about ten days so that she may recover her looks and become herself again. Then send her to the Hammam <term>public bathhouse</term>, dress her in the finest clothing, and go with her to the Sultan: this will be more to your advantage.” 

The Wazir considered the Persian’s words and approved of their wisdom; so he took her to his palace, where he assigned her private rooms and provided her every day with whatever she needed in the way of food, drink, and so on. In this way, she stayed there for a while. Now, the Wazir Al-Fazl had a son who was like the full moon when most beautifully arrayed—his face was radiant with light, his cheeks were a bright ruddy color, and he had a mole like a speck of ambergris <term>a waxy substance used in perfume</term> on his soft skin; as the poet said of him, and said quite rightly:

> A moon which blights you <note>“The sun shall not strike you by day, nor the moon by night” (Psalm 121:6). People in the East still believe in the harmful effects of the moon’s rays, which Northern Europeans, who see the moon under different conditions, choose to deny. I have seen a healthy Arab look like a man fresh from a sickbed after sitting in the moonlight for an hour; and I knew an Englishman in India whose face was temporarily paralyzed because he slept with it exposed to the moon.</note> if you dare to look; * A branch which wraps you in its swaying embrace:

# Nur al-Din Ali and the Young Woman Anis al-Jalis

->Hair like the curls of Africans <note>original: "Zanj"</note> and the golden shimmer of light; ◦ A graceful walk and a figure like a spear to be held:<-
->Ah, hard-hearted one with such a soft and slender waist! ◦ Why not change that cruelty into kindness? <note>Why not make your heart as soft as your body!</note><-
->If the softness of your form were within your heart, ◦ your lover would never find you harsh and cold.<-
->Oh, you who judge me! Excuse my love, ◦ and do not scold me if the pangs of love bring me endless sorrow!<-
->I am not to blame; it is all the fault of my heart and eyes; ◦ so stop your criticism and let me long and ache.<-

Now, the handsome young man <note>Nur al-Din Ali, the Wazir's son</note> was unaware of the young woman's arrival. His father had strictly instructed her, saying, "Understand, my daughter, that I have bought you to be a companion for our King, Muhammad bin Sulayman al-Zayni. I have a son who is a devil when it comes to girls; he does not leave a single young woman in the neighborhood without taking her virginity. So, be on your guard against him, and take care never to let him see your face or hear your voice."

"I hear and obey," the girl replied. He left her and went on his way. 

A few days later, as fate would have it, the girl went to the private baths in the house, where some of the slave women washed her. Afterward, she dressed herself in magnificent clothing, which made her beauty and charm even more radiant. Then she visited the Wazir's wife and kissed her hand. 

The lady said to her, "Blessings on your bath! <note>original: "Na'iman!"</note> May it do you good, Anis al-Jalis! <note>In older versions, she is called "The Fair Persian," likely after her owner. Her name means "The Cheerer of the Companion."</note> Are our baths not beautiful?"

"My mistress," she replied, "I lacked nothing there except your own gracious presence." 

Thereupon the lady said to her slave women, "Come with us to the bathhouse..." <margin>The word "Na'iman" is a blessing said to someone after they have bathed or had their head shaved. The proper response—as every polite gesture in the East has a counter-gesture—is "May Allah benefit you!" I have previously provided examples not only of these gestures but also of the rhyming banter that roguish people enjoy. For example: "May it be pleasant to you!" (said when someone drinks), to which the response is "May Allah give you pleasure!" (though some ruffians twist the words into something vulgar). Other rhyming insults involve calling someone a "hen" or making crude jokes about physical anatomy.</margin>

<summary>The Wazir warns Anis al-Jalis to stay hidden from his lascivious son, Nur al-Din Ali, while she prepares herself to be presented to the King. After a visit to the baths, her beauty is enhanced, and she shares a polite exchange with the Wazir’s wife.</summary>

"...for it has been several days since we last went there." They answered, "To hear is to obey!" <note>original: "Sam'an wa Ta'atan" — a common Arabic expression of compliance</note> and all rose to accompany her. 

Now, she had stationed two young slave-girls to guard the door of the private room where Anis al-Jalis was staying and told them, "Do not allow anyone to enter and see the young woman." Soon, as the beautiful young woman sat resting in her rooms, the Wazir's son—whose name was Nur al-Din Ali¹—suddenly walked in. He asked about his mother and her attendants, to which the two young slave-girls replied, "They are in the baths <note>original: "Hammam"</note>."

But Anis al-Jalis had heard Nur al-Din Ali's voice from inside and said to herself, "Oh, I wish to Heaven I could see what this youth looks like! The Wazir warned me about him, saying he hasn't left a single virgin in the neighborhood without taking her virginity. By God <note>original: "Allah"</note>, I long to see him!" 

So she sprang to her feet, still feeling refreshed from her bath. Stepping to the door, she looked at Nur al-Din Ali and saw a youth as beautiful as the full moon; the sight left her breathless with a thousand sighs. The young man also glanced at her, and that look filled his mind with a thousand anxious thoughts; both of them fell instantly into love's trap. 

Then he stepped toward the two young slave-girls and shouted at them. They both fled from him and stood at a distance to see what he would do. And look, he walked to the door of the young woman's room, opened it, went inside, and asked her, "Are you the one my father bought for me?" She answered, "Yes." 

At that, the youth, who was feeling bold from drinking wine, went up to her and embraced her. He lifted her legs and wrapped them around his waist, and she wound her arms around his neck, meeting him with kisses, murmurs of pleasure, and romantic playfulness. Then they kissed passionately, and finally, he loosened the drawstrings of her trousers and took her virginity <term>abated her maidenhead: took her virginity</term>. 

When the two young slave-girls saw their young master go into Anis al-Jalis's room, they cried out and shrieked. As soon as the youth had satisfied his desires with her, he got up and fled, fearing the consequences of his misbehavior. When the Wazir's wife heard the slave-girls' cries, she sprang up and came out of the baths with sweat pouring from her face, saying, "What is this shameful noise in the house?²" Then she went to the two young slave-girls and asked them, saying:

“Do not kill yourself,” said his wife, “I will give you ten thousand gold coins <term>dinars</term>, her original price, out of my own money.”

> Show me a miser who ever rose to high rank through stinginess, ⋄ Or a generous man whom giving has ever killed.”

"Yes," said Nur al-Din. 

Thereupon the broker went around to the merchants but found that they had not all assembled yet. So he waited until the rest had arrived and the market was crowded with slave-girls of all nations: Turks, Franks, and Circassians; Abyssinians, Nubians, and <term>Takruris</term>; <note>Muslims from Central and Western North Africa. A "Jabarti" refers to a Muslim Abyssinian (Ethiopian).</note> Tartars, Georgians, and others. When he came forward, he stood and cried aloud, "O merchants! O men of money! Every round thing is not a walnut, and every long thing is not a banana; all red things are not meat, nor are all white things fat, nor is every brown thing a date! <note>This is a favorite bit of banter that can be extended indefinitely; for example: not every black thing is charcoal, nor every white thing chalk; not every shiny thing is a diamond, etc.</note> O merchants, I have here this perfect pearl that has no price: at what sum shall I start the bidding for her?" 

"Start the bidding at four thousand five hundred dinars," said one of the traders. 

The broker opened the sale at the named price, and while he was still calling out, the Wazir Al-Mu’in bin Sawi passed through the bazar. Seeing Nur al-Din Ali waiting to one side, he said to himself, "Why is Khakan's son <note>The Wazir refers to him by his grandfather's name, which was a common custom.</note> standing around here? Does this gallows-bird have anything left with which to buy slave-girls?" Then he looked—

He looked around and, seeing the broker calling out in the market with all the merchants gathered around him, said to himself, "I am sure that Nur al-Din is penniless and has brought the young woman Anis al-Jalis here for sale." He added, "Oh, how cooling and grateful is this to my heart!" 

Then he called for the auctioneer, who came up and bowed low, kissing the ground before him. The Wazir said to him, "I want this slave-girl whom you are offering for sale." The broker dared not defy him, so he answered, "O my lord, <term>Bismillah</term>! <note>original: "Bismillah!"—In the name of Allah; a common invocation used when starting a task or agreeing to something.</note> In Allah's name, so be it." He led the young woman forward and showed her to him. 

She pleased him greatly, at which point he asked, "O Hasan, what has been bid for this girl?" 

He answered, "Four thousand five hundred <term>dinars</term> <note>A gold currency.</note> to open the bidding." 

Al-Mu'in said, "Four thousand five hundred is *my* bid." 

When the merchants heard this, they held back and did not dare to bid another <term>dirham</term> <note>A silver currency.</note>, knowing well the Wazir's tyranny, violence, and treachery. So Al-Mu'in looked at the broker and said to him, "Why are you standing still? Go and offer four thousand dinars for me, and the remaining five hundred shall be for yourself." 

Thereupon the broker went to Nur al-Din and said, "O my lord, your slave is going for nothing!" 

"And why is that?" Nur al-Din asked. 

The broker answered, "We had opened the bidding for her at four thousand five hundred dinars. However, when that tyrant, Al-Mu'in bin Sawi, passed through the <term>bazaar</term> <note>A market.</note> and saw the young woman, she pleased him. So he shouted to me: 'Tell the seller the price is four thousand dinars, and you shall have five hundred for yourself.' I have no doubt that he knows the girl is yours. If he would pay you her price in cash immediately, it would be well enough; but I know his injustice and violence. He will give you a written order addressed to one of his agents and will later send word to them, saying, 'Pay him nothing.' So, every time you go in search of your money, they will say, 'We will pay you shortly!' and they will put you off day after day. You are a proud man; eventually, when they are tired of your persistence, they will say, 'Show us the check.' Then, as soon as they have it in their hands, they will tear it up, and you will lose the girl's price entirely." 

When Nur al-Din heard this, he looked at the broker and asked him, "How shall this matter be managed?" 

He answered, "I will give you a piece of advice which, if you follow it, will bring you complete satisfaction." 

"And what is that?" asked Nur al-Din. 

The broker said, "Come to me in a moment while I am standing in the middle of the market. Take the girl from my hand, give her a sound slapping, and say to her: 'You baggage, I have..."

"I kept my vow and brought you down to the slave market, because I swore an oath that I would carry you from home to the bazaar and have the brokers offer you for sale. If you do this, perhaps the trick will deceive the Wazir and the people, and they will believe that you only brought her to the bazaar to fulfill your oath." He replied, "That would be the best way." Then the broker left him and, returning to the center of the market, took the young woman by the hand, gestured to the Wazir, and said, "My lord, here is her owner." At this, Nur al-Din Ali stepped forward and, snatching the girl from the broker's hand, struck her hard and said to her, "Shame on you, you hussy! I have only brought you to the bazaar to fulfill my oath; now go home and stop opposing me as you usually do. Damn you! Do I need the money from your sale, that I should sell you? The furniture in my house is worth many times your price!"

When Al-Mu'in saw this, he said to Nur al-Din, "Curse you! Do you have anything left to sell or buy?" He would have attacked him, but the merchants stepped in (for they all loved Nur al-Din), and the young man said to them, "Here I am in your hands, and you all know his tyranny." "By Allah," cried the Wazir, "if not for these people, I would have killed him!" Then everyone gestured to Nur al-Din with meaningful looks, as if to say, "Take your revenge on him; not one of us will interfere between the two of you." Thereupon Nur al-Din, who was as brave of heart as he was strong of body, went up to the Wazir and, dragging him over the pommel of his saddle, threw him to the ground. Now, in that spot there was a pit for mixing brick clay,¹ and he fell right into the middle of it. Nur al-Din kept punching and pummeling him; one of the blows hit him squarely in the teeth, and his beard was stained with his blood. The minister also had ten armed slaves with him. When they saw their master treated in this way, they put their hands on their sword hilts and were about to draw their blades and attack Nur al-Din to cut him down; but the merchants and bystanders said to them, "This man is a Wazir and the other is the son of a Wazir; perhaps they will make peace eventually, in which case you will lose the favor of both. Or perhaps your master will be killed, and you will all suffer the most shameful deaths; so it

“It would be better for you not to interfere.” Accordingly, they stayed out of it, and when Nur al-Din had finished thrashing the Wazir, he took his handmaid and went home. Al-Mu’in also went his way at once, with his clothing stained three colors: black with mud, red with blood, and gray with brick dust. When he saw himself in this state, he tied a piece of matting <note>Arabic: "Barsh," a piece of round matting used by the poor as a seat. By wearing it, the Wazir signaled that he had been degraded to the lowly status of a mat-maker.</note> around his neck and, carrying two bundles of coarse Halfa grass <note>A type of tough grass that gave its name to Wadi Halfa. The traveler Burckhardt incorrectly translated it as "dry reeds."</note> in his hands, went up to the palace. Standing under the Sultan’s windows, he cried aloud, “O King of the age, I have been wronged! I have been terribly wronged!”

They brought him before the King, who looked at him and saw that it was his chief Minister. The King said, “O Wazir, who did this to you?” Al-Mu’in wept and sobbed, reciting these lines:

->Shall the world oppress me while you are in it?<-
->In the lion’s presence, shall wolves devour?<-
->Shall the parched drink their fill from your tanks,<-
->While I, beneath a rain-cloud, thirst for a cooling shower?<-

“O my lord,” he cried, “the same will happen to everyone who loves and serves you well.” 

“Be quick,” said the Sultan, “and tell me how this happened, and who did this to one whose honor is part of my own honor.” 

The Wazir replied, “Know, my lord, that I went to the slave market today to buy a cook. While there, I saw a young woman—in all my life I have never seen anyone more beautiful. I intended to buy her for our lord the Sultan, so I asked the broker about her and her owner. He answered, ‘She belongs to Ali, son of Al-Fazl ibn Khakan. Some time ago, our lord the Sultan gave his father ten thousand dinars to buy him a beautiful slave girl. He bought this maiden, and she pleased him; so he begrudged giving her to our lord the Sultan and gave her to his own son instead. When the father died, the son sold all his houses, gardens, and household goods, squandering the money until he was penniless. Then he brought the girl to the market to sell her, and he handed her over to the broker to auction off. The merchants bid higher and higher on her until her price reached...’”

### Nur al-Din Ali and the Damsel Anis al-Jalis

...the bidding reached four thousand dinars. At that point, I said to myself, "I will buy this girl for our lord the Sultan, since it was his money that was paid for her." So I said to Nur al-Din, "O my son, sell her to me for four thousand dinars." 

When he heard my words, he looked at me and cried, "You wretched old man! I would sell her to a Jew or to a Christian <note>original: "Nazarene"</note>, but I will never sell her to you!" 

"I am not buying her for myself," I replied, "I am buying her for our lord and benefactor the Sultan." 

Hearing my words, he was filled with rage. Dragging me off my horse—and I am a very old man—he beat me unmercifully with his fists and slapped me with his palms until he left me in the state you see. All this has happened to me only because I intended to buy this girl for you!" 

Then the Wazir threw himself on the ground and lay there weeping and shivering. When the Sultan saw his condition and heard his story, the vein of rage started out between his eyes <note>This "Hashimi" vein, as it was called, was an abnormal development between the eyes of the House of Abbas, inherited from the great-grandfather of the Prophet; it would swell in anger and battle-rage. Alternatively, the text may read "the sweat of wrath."</note>. He turned to his bodyguard who stood before him—forty white slaves, all skilled swordsmen—and said to them, "Go down immediately to the house built by the son of Khakan. Sack it and tear it down, and bring his son Nur al-Din to me along with the girl. Drag them both on their faces with their arms tied behind them!" 

They replied, "To hear is to obey," and after arming themselves, they set out for the house of Nur al-Din Ali. 

Now, there was a Chamberlain <term>A high-ranking official in a royal court</term> near the Sultan named Alam al-Din Sanjar <note>Translators Torrens and Payne prefer "Ilm," meaning knowledge, while Lane more correctly uses "Alam," meaning a sign or flag.</note>. He had previously been a Mameluke <term>A soldier of slave origin who had converted to Islam</term> to Al-Fazl, but he had risen in rank, and the Sultan had promoted him to be one of his Chamberlains. When he heard the King’s command and saw the enemies preparing to kill his old master’s son, he was deeply grieved. He left the Sultan’s presence, mounted his horse, and rode to Nur al-Din’s house. He knocked at the door, and when Nur al-Din came out and recognized him, he tried to greet him. But the Chamberlain said, "O my master, this is no time for greetings or formalities. Listen to what the poet said:

> Flee, flee for your life if misfortune overtakes you!
> Let your house announce your death, abandoned by its builder!
> For you may find another land to replace this one, my brother,
> But you will never find another life in this world. <note>These lines appeared in Night 11; this version follows the translation by Torrens.</note>

"O Alam al-Din, what news?" asked Nur al-Din. He answered, "Get up quickly and flee for your life, you and the young woman; for Al-Mu'in has set a trap for you both. If you fall into his hands, he will kill you. The Sultan has sent forty swordsmen against you, and I advise you to flee before harm can come to you." 

Then Sanjar reached into his purse and, finding forty gold pieces, took them and gave them to Nur al-Din, saying, "O my lord, take these and travel with them. If I had more I would give it to you, but this is no time for excuses." 

Immediately, Nur al-Din went to the young woman and told her what had happened, at which she wrung her hands in distress. They left the city at once, and Allah spread His veil of protection over them so that they reached the riverbank. There, they found a vessel ready for sea. Her captain was standing amidships, shouting, "Whoever has anything to do, whether it is getting supplies or saying goodbye to his people, or whoever has forgotten any necessary thing, let him do it at once and return, for we are about to sail!" 

When everyone replied, "We have nothing left to do, O Captain!", he cried to his crew, "Hey there! Cast off the cable and pull up the mooring pole!"¹ Nur al-Din asked, "Where are you bound, O Captain?" and he replied, "To the House of Peace, Baghdad."

And Shahrazad saw the break of day and stopped her permitted speech.

### Now when it was the **Thirty-sixth Night**,

She said: It has reached me, O auspicious King, that when the captain answered, "To the House of Peace, Baghdad," Nur al-Din Ali and the young woman went on board. They launched the craft and shook out the sails, and the ship sped forth as though she were a bird on the wing; just as someone once said, and said very well:

> Observe a tall ship; she is a joy to behold,
> Outstripping the breeze in her haste to flee;
> Like a bird with wide-spreading wings,
> Leaving the sky to settle on the sea.

# Nur al-Din Ali and the Young Woman Anis al-Jalis

The ship sailed at full speed with a favorable wind. That was the situation for them; meanwhile, the Mamelukes <note>Mamelukes: a class of soldier-slaves who often held high military and political power</note> went to Nur al-Din’s mansion. They broke open the doors, entered, and searched the entire place, but could find no trace of him or the young woman. So, they demolished the house and returned to the Sultan to report what they had done. At this, the Sultan said, "Search for them both, wherever they may be." They answered, "To hear is to obey." 

The Vizier Al-Mu’in had also gone home after the Sultan had presented him with a robe of honor and set his heart at ease by saying, "None shall take <term>blood-vengeance</term> <note>original: "blood-wreak"</note> for you but me." Al-Mu'in had blessed the King and prayed for his long life and prosperity. Then the Sultan ordered a proclamation to be made throughout the city: "Hear ye, all you subjects! It is the will of our lord the Sultan that whoever finds Nur al-Din Ali, son of Al-Fazl bin Khakan, and brings him to the Sultan, shall receive a robe of honor and one thousand gold pieces. Anyone who hides him or knows his whereabouts and does not report it deserves whatever pains and penalties shall befall him." So everyone began to search for Nur al-Din Ali, but they could find neither a trace nor any news of him. 

Meanwhile, he and his handmaid sailed on with a following wind until they arrived safely at Baghdad. The captain said to them, "This is Baghdad, the city where security is to be found. Winter and its frosts have passed, and <term>Spring</term> <note>original: "Prime"</note> has come to display its roses; the flowers are glowing, the trees are blooming, and the streams are flowing." 

So Nur al-Din landed with his handmaid. He gave the captain five dinars and walked on a little way until the decrees of Fate brought them to the gardens. They came to a place that had been swept and sprinkled with water, with benches along the walls and hanging jars filled with water.¹ Overhead was a trellis of reed-work and canes shading the entire length of the avenue, and at the far end was a garden gate, though it was locked. 

"By God," said Nur al-Din to the young woman, "this is a very pleasant place!" 

She replied, "O my lord, sit with me a while on this bench and let us rest." 

So they climbed up and sat down on the bench, where they washed their faces and hands. A cool breeze blew over them and they fell asleep—and glory be to Him who never sleeps!

# The Thousand and One Nights

This garden was named the Garden of Gladness,¹ and within it stood a lookout called the Palace of Pleasure and the Pavilion of Pictures. The entire estate belonged to the Caliph Harun al-Rashid, who was accustomed to visiting the garden and palace to sit whenever his heart was burdened with worry. The palace had eighty latticed windows and eighty lamps hanging around a large gold candelabrum equipped with wax candles. When the Caliph entered, he would order the handmaidens to throw open the lattices and light the rooms, and he would command Ishak bin Ibrahim, his boon companion, and the slave-girls to sing until his spirit was lifted and his troubles were eased.

Now the keeper of the garden, Shaykh Ibrahim, was a very old man. From time to time, when he went out on business, he had found people lounging near the garden gate with their <term>mistresses</term> <note>original: "bona robas"</note>, which made him feel great anger.² However, he remained patient until one day when the Caliph came to his garden; he complained about this to Harun al-Rashid, who said, "Whomever you catch at the door of the garden, deal with them as you wish." 

On this day, the gardener happened to be away on some business, and upon returning, he found these two sleeping at the gate, covered by a single shawl. He said to himself, "By Allah, this is something! These two do not know that the Caliph has given me permission to kill anyone I catch at the door; I will give this couple a severe whipping so that no one else will come near the gate in the future." 

So he cut a green palm-branch³ and approached them. Raising his arm so high that the white of his armpit showed, he was about to strike them when he reconsidered and said, "O Ibrahim, will you beat them without knowing their situation? Perhaps they are strangers or of the Sons [of the Way]..."

...travelers of the road,¹ and the decrees of destiny have thrown them here. I will uncover their faces and look at them." Then he covered their faces again and, going to Nur al-Din's feet, began to rub and massage them,² at which the youth opened his eyes. The gate was arched like a great hall, and over the walls and roof grew climbing vines with grapes of many colors: the red ones looked like rubies and the black ones like ebony. Beyond it lay a bower of trellised branches bearing various fruits, both simple and clustered. Small birds on the branches sang with melodious voices, and the thousand-noted nightingale chirped with her varied cries; the turtle-dove filled the place with her cooing; the blackbird whistled like a human being,³ and the ring-dove moaned like a drinker in deep distress. The trees produced every kind of edible growth in perfection and bore all manner of fruits in pairs. There were camphor-apricots, almond-apricots, and the apricot called <term>Khorasani</term> <note>A variety of apricot originating from the Khorasan region of Iran/Central Asia.</note>. # Alf Laylah wa Laylah (The Thousand and One Nights)

...bright; the cherry that makes teeth shine clearly by its artistry, and the fig of three colors: green, purple, and white. There also blossomed the violet, appearing like burning sulfur in the night; the orange with buds like pink coral and pearls; the rose whose redness makes the loveliest cheeks blush with envy; and myrtle, wallflowers, and lavender with the blood-red anemone named after Nu’man. The leaves were all gemmed with tears provided by the clouds; the chamomile smiled, showing biting teeth, and the Narcissus fixed its dark eyes <note>original: "negro eyes." The translator makes an unpleasant comparison of the classical Narcissus with the yellow-white of a Black person's eyes.</note> upon the Rose. The citrons shone, filled with fruit, and the lemons were like balls of gold; the earth was carpeted with flowers of infinite colors, for Spring had come, brightening the place with joy and delight. The streams ran ringing to the birds’ gay singing, while the rustling breeze arising tempered the air to an exquisite mildness. 

Shaykh Ibrahim led them up into the pavilion, and they gazed on its beauty and on the lamps mentioned before in the latticed windows. Nur al-Din, remembering his parties from the past, cried out, "By Allah, this is a pleasant place; it has quenched the anguish in me which burned like a fire of Ghaza-wood <note>A tree (Artemisia) whose coals burn with fierce heat, characteristic of the Arabian Desert. The traveler and explorer Mr. Palgrave describes it as a woody stem with feathery twigs that provide shelter and food for camels.</note>." 

Then they sat down and Shaykh Ibrahim set food before them; they ate until they were satisfied and washed their hands. After this, Nur al-Din went up to one of the latticed windows and, calling to his handmaid, began to gaze at the trees laden with all kinds of fruit. Presently he turned to the gardener and said to him, "O Shaykh Ibrahim, do you have any drink here? People are accustomed to drinking after eating." 

The Shaykh brought him sweet water, cool and pleasant, but he said, "This is not the kind of drink I wanted." 

"Perhaps you wish for wine?" 

"Indeed I do, O Shaykh!" 

"I seek refuge with Allah from it! It is thirteen years since I have done such a thing, for the Prophet (may Allah bless him and keep him! <note>original: "Abhak," an acronym for the Arabic *Salla Allahu alayhi wa sallam*, meaning "Allah bless him and preserve him."</note>) cursed..."

This way, you will be neither the presser, nor the buyer, nor the carrier, and no part of the curse will fall on you." 

At this, Shaykh Ibrahim laughed and said, "By Allah, my son, I have never seen anyone more clever than you, nor heard anything sweeter than your speech." 

So he did exactly as Nur al-Din told him. Nur al-Din thanked him and said, "We two are now dependent on your hospitality, and it is only right that you comply with our wishes; so bring us what we require." 

"O my son," he replied, "this is my <term>buttery</term> (liquor store-room) before you"—and it was actually the store-room provided for the <term>Commander of the Faithful</term> (the Caliph)—"so go in and take whatever you want, for there is more than enough for your needs." 

Nur al-Din then entered the pantry and found vessels of gold, silver, and crystal set with all kinds of gems. He was amazed and delighted by what he saw. He took out what he needed, set the table, and poured the wine into flagons and glass pitchers, while Shaykh Ibrahim brought them fruit, flowers, and aromatic herbs. 

Then the old man withdrew and sat down at a distance from them while they drank and made merry. Eventually, the wine began to affect them; their cheeks turned red and their eyes sparkled with a wild, playful look. Their hair became dishevelled, and their natural beauty became even more striking. 

Then Shaykh Ibrahim said to himself, "What is wrong with me, that I am sitting apart from them? Why should I not sit with them? When will I ever find myself in the company of two people like these, who resemble two moons?" 

So he stepped forward and sat down on the edge of the <term>dais</term> (raised platform), and Nur al-Din said to him, "My lord, I beg you, come closer to us!" He came and sat by them, when—

### Now when the **Thirty-seventh Night** arrived,

Then he rose to his feet, opened all the lattice windows, and sat down again; they returned to their carousing and reciting verses until the place rang with their noisy mirth. Now Allah, the Decreer who decrees all things and who appoints a cause for every effect, had arranged matters so that the Caliph <note>Harun al-Rashid</note> was at that moment sitting in the moonlight at one of the windows of his palace overlooking the Tigris River. He saw the blaze of the lamps and wax candles reflected in the river; lifting his eyes, he realized it came from the Garden Palace, which was all ablaze with brilliance.

So he cried, "Bring Ja'afar the Barmaki to me!"; and the last word was hardly spoken before the Wazir <term>Minister or high-ranking advisor</term> was present before the Commander of the Faithful <note>A title for the Caliph</note>, who shouted at him, "You dog of a Minister, have you taken the city of Baghdad from me without saying a word to me?"

"What kind of talk is this?" asked Ja'afar.

The Caliph answered, "If the city of Baghdad had not been taken from me, the Palace of Pictures would not be illuminated with lamps and candles, nor would its windows be thrown open. Woe to you! Who would dare do such a thing unless the Caliphate <term>The office and dominion of the Caliph</term> had been taken from me?"

Ja'afar said (and indeed, his muscles trembled as he spoke), "Who told you that the Palace of Pictures was illuminated and the windows thrown open?"

Then Ja'afar came close to the Caliph and, looking toward the garden, saw the palace blazing with light that radiated through the gloom of the night. Thinking that the keeper might have permitted this for some reason of his own, he wanted to make an excuse for him; so he said, "O Commander of the Faithful, Shaykh Ibrahim said to me last week: 'O my lord...'"

> And do not drink without music, for I have often seen ◦ that a horse drinks best to the sound of a whistle!

He descended and stood before the Commander of the Faithful, who said to him, "O Ja'afar, praise be to Allah, who has made us among those who observe the external laws of the Holy Law, and has kept us from the sin of disguising ourselves like hypocrites!"²

<margin>1</margin> Arabic: “Lisám,” the end of the “Kufiyah” (head-kerchief), which is passed over the face under the eyes and fastened on the other side. This mouth-veil serves as a mask (making the eyes unrecognizable) and protects against heat, cold, and thirst. I also believe that hooding the eyes with this garment in the Bedouin <note>original: "Badawi"</note> style produces a sensation of coolness, or at least a marked difference in perceived temperature; somewhat like wearing a pair of dark spectacles or looking at the sea from a sandy shore. See *Pilgrimage* volume 1, pages 210 and 346. The woman’s “Lisám” (chin-veil) or Yashmak is mentioned in volume 1, page 337.

Flee for your life, for the Caliph is in the garden tonight and, if he sees you, your head is as good as gone.” At this, the Caliph laughed and Ja’afar recognized him. He asked, “Can it be you, our lord the Sultan?” and he answered, “Yes, O Ja’afar, and you are my <term>Vizier</term> and yet you and I came here together and you did not know me. So how should Shaykh Ibrahim recognize me while he is drunk? Stay here until I come back to you.” “To hear is to obey,” said Ja’afar. Then the Caliph went up to the door of the pavilion and knocked gently, at which Nur al-Din said, “O Shaykh Ibrahim, someone is tapping at the door.” “Who goes there?” cried the Shaykh, and the Caliph replied, “It is I, O Shaykh Ibrahim!”

---

<note>¹ The most notable aspect of this story is the familiarity between the most powerful man in the world at that time and his impoverished subject. The fisherman refers to an Islamic practice, established by Caliph Omar, that all rulers should work at some manual craft in order to avoid draining the public treasury. Because of this, Sultan Mu’ayyad of Cairo was a calligrapher who sold his own handwriting, and his example was followed by the Turkish Sultans Mahmúd, Abd al-Majíd, and Abd al-Aziz. German royalty often preferred carpentry, while Louis XVI practiced watchmaking.</note>

"Who are you?" he asked, and the other replied, "I am Karim the fisherman. I heard you are having a feast, so I have brought you some fish, and truly they are good fish." When Nur al-Din heard the mention of fish, both he and the damsel were glad. They both said to the Shaykh, "O our lord, open the door and let him bring us his fish." So Shaykh Ibrahim opened the door and the Caliph came in, disguised as a fisherman, and began by saluting them. 

Shaykh Ibrahim said, "Welcome to the scoundrel, the robber, and the gambler! Let us see your fish." So the Caliph showed them his catch and, behold, the fish were still alive and jumping. At this, the damsel exclaimed, "By God! <note>original: "By Allah"</note> My lord, these are indeed fine fish; I wish they were fried!" 

Shaykh Ibrahim replied, "By God, my lady, you are right." Then he said to the Caliph, "Fisherman, why didn't you bring us the fish already fried? Get up now, cook them, and bring them back to us." 

"I am at your command!" said the Caliph. "I will fry a dish for you and bring it." 

They told him, "Hurry up." 

Thereupon he went out and ran until he reached Ja’afar, calling out, "Hello, Ja'afar!" 

He replied, "Here I am, O Commander of the Faithful. Is all well?" 

"They want the fish fried," said the Caliph. 

Ja’afar answered, "O Commander of the Faithful, give them to me and I will fry them for them." 

"By the tombs of my ancestors," the Caliph said, "no one shall fry them but me, with my own hands!" 

So he went to the gardener’s hut, where he searched and found all that he required, including salt, saffron, wild marjoram, and more. Then he turned to the <term>brasier: a portable heater or grill used for cooking</term> and, setting on the frying pan, prepared a very good fry. When it was done, he laid it on a banana leaf and, gathering fallen fruit from the garden—limes and lemons—he carried the fish to the pavilion and set the dish before them. 

The youth, the damsel, and Shaykh Ibrahim came forward and ate. Afterward, they washed their hands and Nur al-Din said to the Caliph, "By God, fisherman, you have done us a very good deed tonight." Then he reached into his purse and, taking out three of the <term>dinars: gold coins</term> that Sanjar had given him, said, "Fisherman, please excuse me. By God, if I had known you before my recent troubles, I would have removed the bitterness of poverty from your heart; but take this as the best I can do for you." 

Then he threw the gold pieces to the Caliph, who took them, kissed them, and put them in his pocket. Now, his only goal in doing all this was to hear the damsel sing; so he said to Nur al-Din, "You have rewarded me most generously, but I beg of your boundless..."

So *Nur al-Din* said, "O *Anis al-Jalis*!" and she answered, "Yes!" 
and he continued, "By my life, sing us something for the sake of this fisherman who wishes so much to hear you." Thereupon she took the lute and struck the strings after she had tightened and tuned them, and she sang these improvised verses:

A maiden, graceful as a fawn, took her lute in hand, 
And her music made us truly spirited;
For her song gave hearing to ears stone-deaf,
While even the mute cried out, "*Brava! Brava!*"

Then she played again, and played so delightfully that she enchanted their minds; she broke into improvisation and sang these couplets:

You have honored us by visiting our land,
And your splendor has lit up the gathering shadows;
So it is only right that I perfume my home for you
With rose-water, musk, and the scent of camphor!

At this, the Caliph was deeply moved, and emotion so overcame him that he could not control himself for sheer pleasure. He exclaimed, "By God, that is good! By God, it is good! By God, it is good!" <note>original: "Wa’lláhi tayyib!"—an exclamation typical of Egyptian Muslims.</note>
*Nur al-Din* asked, "O fisherman, does this young woman please you?" 
and the Caliph answered, "Yes, by God!" 
Whereupon *Nur al-Din* said, "She is a gift to you—the gift of a generous man who does not regret his giving and who will never take back his gift!" 
Then he sprang to his feet and, taking a loose robe, threw it over the fisherman and told him to take the young woman and go. 
But she looked at him and said, "O my lord, are you going away without a farewell? If it must be so, at least stay until I say goodbye and explain my situation." And she began to put her feelings into these verses:

When love and longing and regret are all mine,
Must not this body show signs of illness?
My love! Do not say, "You will soon be comforted";
When one heart speaks to another, nothing shall soothe my grief.
If a living man could swim upon his tears,
I would be the first to float upon the waters of these eyes:

When he had ended his poem, the Caliph said to him, “O my lord Nur al-Din, explain your situation to me more fully.” So he told him the whole story from beginning to end, and the Caliph asked him, “Where do you intend to go now?” “God’s world is wide,” he replied. The Caliph said, “I will write a letter for you to take to Sultan Mohammed bin Sulayman al-Zayni. When he reads it, he will not hurt or harm you in any way.” — And Shahrazad saw the dawn of day and stopped speaking her permitted words.

¹ Such an act of generosity would seem almost like insanity to Europeans, but it is quite consistent with Arab customs. Look at the frequently quoted story of Hatim and his horse. As a rule, the Arab is the opposite of generous, contrasting poorly in this regard with his cousin the Jew; therefore, his ideal of generosity is of the highest level. “The generous (meaning the liberal) is God’s friend, even if he is a sinner; and the miser is God’s enemy, even if he is a saint!” Indian Muslims call a miser *Makhi-chus* = fly-sucker <note>See *Pilgrimage* i. 242.</note>.

### Now when it was the Thirty-eighth Night,

She continued: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when the Caliph said to Nur al-Din Ali, “I will write you a letter to carry to Sultan Mohammed bin Sulayman al-Zayni; when he reads it, he will not hurt or harm you in any way,” Nur al-Din asked, “What! Is there a fisherman in the world who writes to Kings? Such a thing can never be!” The Caliph answered, “You speak the truth, but I will tell you the reason. Know that he and I learned in the same school under one schoolmaster, and I was his monitor <term>monitor: a senior student appointed to assist the teacher and oversee other students</term>. Since 그 time, Fortune has befriended him and he has become a Sultan, while Allah has humbled me and made me a fisherman; yet I never send to him to ask for anything but that he fulfills my desire. In fact, even if I were to ask him for a thousand favors every day, he would comply.” When Nur al-Din heard this, he said, “Fine! Write it so that I may see.” So the Caliph took an ink-case and a reed pen and wrote as follows:

> “In the name of Allah, the Compassionating, the Compassionate! To proceed: <note>original: "Ammá ba ’ad"; this is a traditional Arabic transition formula used in formal letters to move from the opening prayer to the main subject.</note> This letter is written by Harun al-Rashid, son of Al-Mahdi, to his highness Mohammed bin Sulayman al-Zayni, whom I have surrounded with my favor and appointed as my viceroy in certain parts of my dominions. The bearer of this letter is Nur al-Din Ali, son of Fazl bin Khakan the Wazir. As soon as this reaches your hand, immediately divest yourself of your royal dignity and invest him with it; do not oppose my command. Peace be with you.”

He gave the letter to Nur al-Din, who took it and kissed it, then placed it in his turban and set out at once on his journey.

So much for him; but as for the Caliph, Shaykh Ibrahim stared at him (while he was still in his fisherman's clothes) and said, “O most wretched of fishermen, you have brought us a couple of fish worth about twenty half-dirhams, <note>original: "Nusf" = half (a dirham). It is the smallest Egyptian coin, made of very base metal; with forty to the piastre, it is worth nearly a quarter of a farthing.</note> and have received three—

---

<note>
1. Arabic: *Ammá ba ’ad* (or *Wa ba ’ad*), an introductory formula attributed to Koss ibn Sa ’idat al-Iyadi, bishop of Najrán (a town in Yemen) and a famous preacher in Muhammad’s day; hence the proverb “more eloquent than Koss.” He was the first to address letters with the heading, “from A. to B.”; and the first who preached from a pulpit while leaning on a sword or a staff. Many Muslims believe the phrase *Ammá ba ’ad* originated with the Prophet David, based on a passage in the Quran (38:19).
</note>

<note>
2. Arabic: “Nusf” means “half” (of a dirham). It is commonly pronounced “nuss,” and is synonymous with the Egyptian “Faddah” (meaning silver), the Greek Asper, and the Turkish “paráh.”
</note>

When the Caliph heard this, he shouted at him and signaled to Masrur, who revealed himself and rushed at him. The man went and, returning with the suit, kissed the ground before the Caliph and gave it to him. Then he threw off the clothes he was wearing <note>The translators Torrens and Lane, being too literal, have the Caliph give the garden boy the clothes he was wearing at the time, forgetting—as did the author or copyist—that he was wearing the fisherman’s filthy suit.</note> and put on kingly apparel. Shaykh Ibrahim was still sitting in his chair, and the Caliph waited to see what would happen next. But seeing the "fisherman" become the Caliph, Shaykh Ibrahim was completely stunned. He could do nothing but bite his fingertips <note>A sign of confusion or disappointment; this is not "biting his nails," which is a European habit and not typically seen in this context in Asia.</note> and say, "I wish I knew whether I am awake or asleep!" At last, the Caliph looked at him and cried out, "O Shaykh Ibrahim, what is this state I find you in?" Thereupon, he recovered from his drunkenness and, throwing himself upon the ground, recited these verses:

> Pardon the sinful ways I did pursue; ◦ Pity <term>ruth: pity or compassion</term> from his lord to every slave is due:
> Confession pays the debt that sin demands; ◦ Where then is that for which grace and mercy plead? <note>Similar lines appear in Night 13; the sentiment is common.</note>

The Caliph forgave him and ordered the young woman to be taken to the city palace, where he set aside an apartment for her and appointed slaves to serve her. He said to her, "Know that we have sent your lord to be Sultan in Basra and, if Almighty Allah wills it, we will send him the robes of office and send you to join him."

Meanwhile, Nur al-Din Ali traveled without stopping until he reached Basra, where he went to the Sultan’s palace and shouted a loud cry. <note>Arabs will still stand beneath a ruler's palace and shout aloud to attract attention. Sayyid Sa'id, known as the 'Imam of Muscat,' used to encourage this patriarchal practice. Muhammad repeatedly protested against such informal conduct (Koran 49:4, etc.). The 'three times of privacy' (Koran 24:58—noted as 105:57 in the original text) are before the dawn prayer, during the midday nap, and after the evening prayer.</note> The Sultan heard him and sent for him. The Sultan said, "I hear and I obey Allah Almighty and the Commander of the Faithful!" Then he summoned the four Kazis <note>The judges of the four orthodox schools of Islamic law.</note> and the Emirs, and he was about to abdicate his royal rule. But just then, Al-Mu’in bin Sawi entered. The Sultan gave him the Caliph's letter. Al-Mu’in read it, then tore it to pieces, put it in his mouth, chewed it <note>He did this so that no one might ever see it or find it again.</note>, and spat it out.

"Shame on you!" said the Sultan (who was indeed very angry). "What possessed you to do such a thing?"

"By your life, O our lord the Sultan!" Al-Mu’in replied. "This man has never met with the Caliph or with his Vizier. He is a rogue destined for the gallows, a limb of Satan, a scoundrel who found a piece of paper with the Caliph’s handwriting—some useless scroll—and used it for his own ends. The Caliph would certainly not send him to take the Sultanate from you without the royal signature <term>Khatt Sharif: a royal autographed letter; the term is still used in Turkey</term> and the formal document of investiture. He surely would have sent a Chamberlain or a Minister with him. But he has come alone, and he never came from the Caliph—never, never, never!"

"What should be done?" asked the Sultan.

The Minister answered, "Leave him to me. I will take him and keep him away from you, and then send him to Baghdad in the custody of a Chamberlain. Then, if what he says is the truth, they will bring us the royal signature and the appointment documents. If not, I will take what is owed to me from this debtor."

When the Sultan heard the Minister's words, he said, "Go then, and take him with you."

Al-Mu’in took custody of him from the King and, bringing him to his own house, shouted to his servants, who laid him flat and beat him until he fainted. Then he put heavy shackles on his feet and took him to the jail. There he called the jailor, a man named Kutayt <note>Meaning "Little Tom-cat"; a diminutive of "Kitt," or "Kutt."</note>, who came and bowed low before him.

The Vizier said, "O Kutayt, I want you to take this fellow and throw him into one of the underground cells <term>Matmurah: an underground silo or cell; the origin of the term "matamor."</term> in the prison and torture him day and night."

"To hear is to obey," replied the jailor. He took Nur al-Din into the prison and locked the door. Then he ordered his men to sweep a bench behind the door. Spreading a rug and a leather cloth on it, he seated Nur al-Din there, removed his shackles, and treated him kindly. The

The Vizier sent word every day commanding the jailer to beat Nur al-Din, but the jailer refused to do so. He continued this kindness for forty days. On the forty-first day, a gift arrived from the Caliph. When the Sultan saw it, he was pleased and consulted his Ministers on the matter. One of them suggested, "Perhaps this gift was intended for the new Sultan." Al-Mu’in cried out, "We would have done well if we had executed him the moment he arrived!" The Sultan exclaimed, "By God, you have reminded me of him! Go down to the prison and fetch him; I will strike off his head." 

"To hear is to obey," replied Al-Mu’in. Then he stood up and said, "I will make a public announcement in the city: 'Whoever wishes to satisfy themselves by watching the beheading of Nur al-Din bin al-Fazl bin Khakan, let them come to the palace!' Everyone, high and low, will flock to the spectacle, and I shall heal my heart and destroy my enemy." 

"Do as you wish," said the Sultan. 

The Vizier went off, feeling glad and cheerful, and ordered the Chief of Police to make the announcement. When the people heard the herald, they all felt sorrow and wept—even the children at school and the merchants in their shops. Some struggled to find good places to watch the execution, while others went to the prison to escort him from there. 

Soon, the Vizier arrived at the jail with ten Mamelukes <term>Mamelukes: elite soldier-slaves who often served as guards or officers</term>. Kutayt the jailer asked him, "Whom do you seek, my lord Vizier?" 

The Vizier answered, "Bring me that criminal destined for the gallows." 

The jailer replied, "He is in a wretched state because of the many beatings I have given him." 

Then the jailer went into the prison and found Nur al-Din reciting these verses:

> Who shall support me in these disasters, ◦ When all cures fail and greater cares arise?
> Exile has worn out my heart and torn my soul; ◦ The world has turned my firmest allies into enemies.
> O people, will not even one friend among you ◦ Mourn my sorrows and cry out when hearing my screams?
> Death and its agonies seem light to me now, ◦ Since life has lost all joy and happiness.
> O Lord of Muhammad <note>original: "Mustafá"</note>, that sea of knowledge, ◦ The sole intercessor and all-wise guide!
> I pray You, free me and forgive my faults, ◦ And drive away from me this evil and my grief.

> The Chosroes <note>original: "Kisras" — Persian Kings</note> and Caesars of a bygone day 
> Stored up wealth; where is it now, and oh, where are they?”

“O Ali,” the Vizier replied, “do you think to frighten me with such talk? I intend this very day to strike off your head <term>smite thy neck: to decapitate</term> despite the protests of the people of Basra <note>original: "Bassorah"</note>, and I do not care; let the days do as they please. I will not turn to your counsel but rather to what the poet says:

> Let the days bring their harm and hatred, 
> And make yourself strong to bear the weight of Fate.

And also as another says so excellently:

> Whoever shall see the death-day of his foe, 
> And survives even one day longer, has won his greatest wish.”

Then he ordered his attendants to mount Nur al-Din upon the bare back of a mule. They said to the youth (for truly this task was hateful to them), “Let us stone the Vizier and cut him down even if our lives are lost for it.” 

But Nur al-Din said to them, “Do not do so; have you not heard the saying of the poet?

> I must endure the term decreed by Fate, 
> And when that day is ended, I must die; 
> If lions dragged me to their forest lair, 
> I would live safely until my day of death draws near.”

Then they proceeded to proclaim before Nur al-Din, “This is the least of the punishment for him who deceives Kings with forgeries.” They did not stop parading him around Basra until they made him stand beneath the palace windows and set him upon the leather of blood <term>leather of blood: a "Nat'a," a leather mat used for executions</term>, and the executioner <term>sworder: a headsman</term> came up to him.

# THE TALE OF GHANIM BIN AYYUB¹, THE DISTRAUGHT, THE SLAVE OF LOVE.

It has reached me, O auspicious King, that in times of old and in years and ages long past, there lived in Damascus a merchant among merchants. He was a wealthy man who had a son as beautiful as the moon on the night of its fullness² and who was also sweet-spoken; he was named Ghanim bin Ayyub, nicknamed "the Distraught, the Slave of Love." He also had a daughter, Ghanim’s own sister, who was called Fitnah, a young woman unique in beauty and loveliness. Their father died and left them abundant wealth—And Shahrazad perceived the dawn of day and ceased to say her permitted say.

->Now when it was the Thirty-ninth Night,<-

She said: It has reached me, O auspicious King, that the merchant left his two children abundant wealth, including one hundred loads³ of silks and fabrics, musk-pods, and mother-of-pearl. On every bale was written, "This is among the packages intended for Baghdad," as it had been his intention to travel there when Almighty Allah took him to Himself; this occurred during the time of the Caliph Harun al-Rashid.

---

¹ Ayyub is the same name as "Job." The English translators of the Bible, who borrowed Martin Luther’s system of transliteration (from 1522 AD), transferred the German "j" into English, which has the sound of "i" or "y." They intended for us to pronounce it "Yakob" (for Jacob), "Yericho," "Yimnites," "Yob" (or Hiob), and "Judah." William Tyndale, who followed Luther (1525–26 AD), preserved the true sound by writing Iacob, Ben Iamin, and Iudas. However, his successors unfortunately returned to the German style; since the 13th century, the initial "I" was ornamentally lengthened and curved to the left, becoming a consonant. The public adopted the local sound of "j" (as in "dg"), and consequently, our language and literature are marred by such distortions as "Jehovah" and "Jesus"—pronounced "Dgehovah" and "Dgeesus" instead of "Yehovah" and "Yesus." Future generations of teachers may fix this error; in the meantime, we are destined for the rest of our days to hear:

->Gee-rusalem! Gee-rusalem! etc.<-

There is not a single word to be said in favor of this corruption, except that—much like the Protestant mispronunciation of Latin and the poor articulation of Greek <note>original: "Erasmian ill-articulation of Greek"</note>—it has become "English," and has played its small part in separating the British from the rest of the civilized world.
² The moon, I repeat, is masculine in the so-called "Semitic" tongues.
³ That is, camel-loads of about 300 pounds; for long journeys, they were about 250 pounds.

After a short time, his son took the loads and, saying goodbye to his mother, relatives, and fellow townspeople, set out with a company of merchants. There, he hired a beautiful house for himself, which he furnished with carpets, cushions, curtains, and hangings. He stored his bales of goods there and stabled his mules and camels, after which he stayed for a while to rest. 

Soon, the merchants and prominent citizens of Baghdad came to greet him. Afterward, he took a bundle containing ten pieces of costly fabrics with the prices written on them and carried it to the merchants' bazaar. There, they welcomed and greeted him, showing him every honor. They helped him dismount from his animal and seated him in the shop of the Syndic <term>the head of the market guild</term> of the market, to whom he delivered the package. The Syndic opened it and, drawing out the pieces of fabric, sold them for him at a profit of two dinars for every dinar of the original cost. Ghanim rejoiced at this and continued selling his silks and fabrics one after another; he did not stop doing business in this way for an entire year. 

On the first day of the following year, he went as was his custom to the Exchange in the bazaar, but he found the gate shut. When he asked why, he was told, "One of the merchants has died, and all the others have gone to follow his funeral procession <note>original: "Janázah," so called only when carrying a corpse; otherwise Na'ash, Sarír, or Tábút. Irán is the large hearse on which chiefs are carried. It is made of plank or stick-work; but there are several varieties.</note>. Why should you not also earn the reward for good deeds by walking with them? <note>It is considered a virtuous act to accompany a Muslim funeral procession, even for just a short distance.</note>" 

He replied, "Yes," and asked for the quarter where the funeral was taking place, and someone directed him there. So, he purified himself by performing ritual washing <note>Wudu-ablution; without this, he could not have joined in the prayers.</note> and went with the other merchants to the prayer hall, where they prayed over the dead. They then walked before the coffin to the burial place. Ghanim, who was a shy man, followed them because he was ashamed to leave their company. 

They eventually left the city and passed through the tombs until they reached the grave. There, they found that the deceased's family had set up a tent over the tomb and had brought lamps and wax candles. They buried the body and sat down while the reciters read and chanted the Quran <term>Koran</term> over the grave. Ghanim sat with them, overcome with shyness and saying to himself, "I cannot easily leave until they do." They stayed there, listening to the recitation...

# TALE OF THE FIRST EUNUCH, BUKHAYT.

KNOW, my brothers, that when I was a small child, about five years old, I was taken from my home country by a slave-trader who sold me to a certain Apparitor <note>original: "Jáwish," a type of official or messenger</note>.^1 My buyer had a daughter three years old, with whom I was raised. They used to treat me like a toy, letting me play with her, dance for her,^2 and sing to her. This continued until I reached the age of twelve and she was ten; even then, they did not forbid me from seeing her. One day I went in to see her and found her sitting in an inner room. She looked as if she had just come out of the bath that was in the house, for she was scented with perfumes and the fragrance of aromatic woods, and her face shone like the full moon on its fourteenth night. She began to play with me, and I with her. Since I had just reached the age of puberty, I became physically aroused. Then she threw me on my back and, sitting astride my chest, moved back and forth upon me until she had uncovered my private parts. When she saw me aroused, she took me in her hand and began rubbing it against her own body^3 outside her undergarments. At that, intense lust was stirred in me and I threw my arms—

# TALE OF THE SECOND EUNUCH, KAFUR.

Know, O my brothers, that when I began my service as a boy of eight, I used to tell the slave-dealers exactly one lie every year. This caused them to quarrel with one another, until at last my master lost patience with me. Taking me down to the market, he ordered the brokers to announce, “Who will buy this slave, knowing his blemish and making allowance for it?” They did so, and the buyers asked him, “Please, what is his blemish?” He answered, “He tells me one single lie every year.” 

Then a merchant came up and said to the broker, “How much do they ask for him with his blemish?” 

“They will accept six hundred <term>dirhams</term> <note>A silver coin used in Islamic states.</note>,” he replied. 

The merchant said, “You shall have twenty dirhams for yourself.” 

So he settled the deal between the merchant and the slave-dealer, who took the money from him. The broker took me to the merchant’s house and departed after receiving his commission. The trader dressed me in suitable clothes, and I stayed in his service for the rest of my first year, until the new year began happily. 

It was a blessed season, with a plentiful harvest, and the merchants used to feast every day at the house of one of their colleagues. Eventually, it was my master’s turn to entertain them in a flower garden outside the city. So he and the other merchants went to the garden, taking with them everything they required for <term>provisions</term> <note>original: "provaunt"</note> and more besides. They sat eating, carousing, and drinking until midday. Then my master, needing something from his home, said to me, “O slave, mount the she-mule and hurry to the house. Bring such and such a thing from your mistress and return quickly.” 

I obeyed his command and started for the house. However, as I drew near it, I began to cry out and shed tears. Because of this, all the people of the neighborhood gathered, both great and small. My master’s wife and daughters, hearing the noise I was making, opened the door and asked me what was the matter. 

I said, “My master was sitting with his friends beneath an old wall, and it fell on every one of them! When I saw what had happened to them, I mounted the mule and came here in haste to tell you.”

# Tale of the Second Eunuch, Kafur.

Laborers with spades and baskets followed my trail, with many people behind them. I ran on ahead of them, howling, throwing dust on my head, and beating my face, followed by my mistress and her children wailing for the dead. But I got ahead of them and entered the garden first. When my master saw me in this state—slapping my face and saying, “Woe is me! My mistress! Alas! Alas! Alas! Who is left to take pity on me now that my mistress is gone? I wish I had died in her place!”—he stood aghast. His face turned pale <term>waxed yellow</term>, and he said to me, “What is wrong with you, O Kafur? What is the matter?”

“O my lord,” I replied, “when you sent me to the house, I found that the wall of the main hall had collapsed and fallen right on top of my mistress and her children!”

“And did your mistress not escape?” 

“No, by God <note>original: "Allah"</note>, O my master; not one of them was saved. The first to die was my mistress, your eldest daughter!” 

“And did my younger daughter not escape?” 

“No, she did not!” 

“And what became of the mule I usually ride? Is she safe?” 

“No, by God <note>original: "Allah"</note>, O my master. The house walls and the stable walls buried every living thing that was inside, even the sheep, geese, and poultry, so that they all became a heap of flesh. The dogs and cats are eating them, and not one of them is left alive.” 

“And did your master, my eldest son, not escape?” 

“No, by God <note>original: "Allah"</note>! Not one of them was saved. Now there is nothing left of the house or the household—not even a trace of them. And as for the sheep, geese, and hens, the cats and dogs have devoured them.”

Love for her now occupied his heart, and he traveled home with her rejoicing, for she was a girl worth ten thousand gold pieces, and her clothing and jewelry would sell for a fortune. As soon as he arrived at his house, he carried in the chest and, opening it——

And Shahrazad perceived the dawn of day and ceased to say her permitted say.

# The Tale of Ghanim bin Ayyub

...fair youth; so when she saw him, she loved him and said, “O my lord, bring us something to eat.” 

“On my head and my eyes!” <note>A traditional Arabic expression of willing service.</note> he replied. Going down to the bazaar, he bought a roasted lamb, a dish of sweets, dried fruits, wax candles, and whatever else was required for drinking, not forgetting perfumes. With all these supplies, he returned to the house. When the young woman saw him, she laughed, kissed him, and threw her arms around his neck. Then she began caressing him, which made his love grow more intense until it completely mastered his heart. They ate and drank, and each felt the deepest affection for the other, for indeed they were both of an age and equal in beauty. 

When night came, Ghanim bin Ayyub—the Distraught, the Slave of Love—rose and lit the wax candles and lamps until the place blazed with light;¹ after this, he brought out the wine service and set the table. Then they both sat down again, and he kept filling her glass while she kept filling his. They played, flirted, laughed, and recited verses while their joy increased, and they clung to each other in deepening love (glory be to the Uniter of Hearts!). They did not stop feasting in this manner until near dawn, when drowsiness overcame them and they slept where they were—apart from one another—until morning.² 

Then Ghanim arose and, going to the market, bought all they required: meat, vegetables, wine, and everything else. He brought them to the house, and they both sat down to eat their fill. When he served the wine, they drank and played together until their cheeks flushed red and their eyes grew dark and heavy. Ghanim’s soul longed to kiss the girl and lie with her, and he said, “O my lady, grant me one kiss from that dear mouth; perhaps it will quench the fire in my heart.” 

“O Ghanim,” she replied, “wait until I am drunk and dead to the world; then steal a kiss from me secretly, in such a way that I may not know you have kissed me.” Then she rose, took off her outer dress, and sat in a thin shift of fine linen and a silken head-kerchief.³ At this, passion inflamed Ghanim, and he said to her, “O my lady, will...”

“And what is the obstacle?” he asked. 

She answered, “Tonight I will tell you my story, so that you may accept my excuse.” 

Then she threw herself upon him and, winding her arms like a necklace about his neck, she kissed and caressed him, promising him her favors. They did not stop playing and laughing until love took the firmest hold upon both their hearts. And so it continued for a whole month, with both of them passing the night on a single mattress; but whenever he tried to enjoy her, she put him off, even as their mutual love grew.
