### The Tale of Ghanim bin Ayyub

Their desire for one another grew until they could hardly resist each other. One night, as he lay by her side and both were tipsy with wine, Ghanim passed his hand over her breasts and stroked them; then he slipped his hand down to her waist as far as her navel. She awoke and, sitting up, put her hand to her trousers. Finding them securely tied, she fell asleep once more. Shortly after, he felt her again and, sliding his hand down to her waistband, began pulling at it, at which point she awoke and sat upright.

Ghanim also sat up beside her, and she asked him, "What do you want?" 

"I want to sleep with you," he answered, "and I want us to deal openly and frankly with each other." 

She replied, "I must now explain my situation to you, so that you may know my rank; then my secret will be disclosed to you and my excuse will become clear." 

"So be it!" he said. 

At that, she opened the hem of her tunic and, taking up her waistband, said to him, "O my lord, read what is embroidered on the flat of this string." 

He took it in his hand and saw these words embroidered on it in gold: **"I AM YOURS, AND YOU ARE MINE, O COUSIN OF THE PROPHET!"** <note>original: "Cousin of the Apostle." This refers to the Abbasid Caliphs, who descended from Al-Abbas, the paternal uncle of Muhammad. The text means more explicitly, "O descendant of the Prophet's uncle!"</note> 

When he read this, he withdrew his hand and said to her, "Tell me who you are!" 

"So be it," she answered. "Know that I am one of the concubines of the Commander of the Faithful <note>The Caliph</note>, and my name is Kut al-Kulub—the Food of Hearts. I was raised in his palace, and when I grew into a woman, he looked at me and, noting the beauty and loveliness the Creator had given me, loved me with an exceeding love. He assigned me a separate apartment and gave me ten slave-girls to wait on me, as well as all these ornaments you see me wearing. 

One day, he set out for one of his provinces, and the Lady Zubaydah <note>The Caliph's primary wife</note> came to one of my servant girls and said to her: 'I have something to ask of you.' 

'What is it, my lady?' the girl asked. 

The Caliph’s wife answered: 'When your mistress Kut al-Kulub is asleep, put this piece of bhang <note>A narcotic preparation of cannabis</note> into her nostrils or drop it into her drink, and I will give you as much money as will satisfy you.' 

'With love and gladness,' the girl replied. She took the bhang from her, being happy because of the money and because she had previously been one of Zubaydah's slaves. So she put the bhang in my drink, and when night came, I drank it. The drug had no sooner settled in my stomach than..."

### Now when it was the Forty-second Night,

[The Caliph learned that Kut al-Kulub] had been in Ghanim’s house for four months. At this, he was filled with overwhelming rage. Rising up, he summoned the <term>Emirs</term> <note>high-ranking military commanders or local governors</note> of his state; his <term>Wazir</term> <note>a high-ranking political advisor or minister; a Vizier</note> Ja'afar the Barmaki also arrived and bowed low, kissing the ground before him. The Caliph said to him in a fury, "Go now, Ja'afar, with a party of armed men and find the house of Ghanim, son of Ayyub. Attack it, plunder it, and bring him to me along with my slave-girl, Kut al-Kulub, for I must certainly punish him!" 

"To hear is to obey," said Ja'afar. Setting out with the Governor, the guards, and a great crowd of people, he headed for Ghanim’s house. 

Now, around that time, the young man happened to have brought home a pot of prepared meat. He and Kut al-Kulub were just about to reach out and eat it when the lady, looking out, saw disaster surrounding the house on every side. The Vizier, the Governor, the night guards, and the <term>Mamelukes</term> <note>a class of warrior-slaves</note> with drawn swords had surrounded it as the white of the eye surrounds the black. 

At this, she knew that news of her had reached the Caliph, her master. She felt certain of her ruin; her face turned pale, her beautiful features twisted with fear, and her charm faded. Then she turned to Ghanim and said to him, "Oh my love, flee for your life!" 

"What shall I do," he asked, "and where shall I go, seeing that all my money and my means of survival are in this house?" 

She answered, "Do not delay, or you will be killed and lose your life as well as your wealth." 

"Oh my beloved and the light of my eyes!" he cried. "How can I get away when they have surrounded the house?" 

She said, "Do not fear." She stripped off his fine clothes and dressed him in ragged old garments. Then she took the pot, put pieces of broken bread and a saucer of meat inside it <note>original: "Ta'ám," which has many meanings: in modern speech it would signify <term>millet</term> or <term>sorghum</term> seed.</note>, and placed it all in a basket. Setting it upon his head, she said, "Go out in this disguise and do not fear for me; I know very well how to handle the Caliph." <note>original: "wotteth right well what thing is in my hand for the Caliph."</note>

So he went out among them, carrying the basket and its contents. The Protector granted him His protection, and he escaped the traps and perils that beset him, thanks to the blessing of his good conscience and pure conduct. Meanwhile, Ja'afar dismounted and, entering the house, saw Kut al-Kulub. She had dressed and adorned herself in splendid robes and jewelry and had filled a chest with gold, jewels, precious stones, and rare items.

"By Allah, O my lady," answered Ja'afar, "the Caliph gave me an order to seize Ghanim, son of Ayyub." 

She replied, "O my lord, he prepared his goods and set out with them for Damascus, and I know nothing more of him. But I ask you to take charge of this chest and deliver it to me in the harem of the Prince of the Faithful." 

"I hear and obey," said Ja'afar. He ordered his men to carry the chest away to the headquarters of the Caliphate along with Kut al-Kulub, commanding them to treat her with honor as someone held in high regard. They did as he commanded after they had wrecked and plundered Ghanim's house. 

Then Ja'afar went to the Caliph and told him everything that had happened. The Caliph ordered Kut al-Kulub to be imprisoned in a dark room and appointed an old woman to serve her, for he was convinced that Ghanim had seduced her and slept with her. Then he wrote an official order to the <term>Emir</term> <note>a high-ranking military commander or governor</note> Mohammed bin Sulayman al-Zayni, his viceroy in Damascus, stating: "The moment you receive this letter of ours, seize Ghanim, son of Ayyub, and send him to us." 

When the letter reached the viceroy, he kissed it and placed it on his head out of respect. Then he had a proclamation made in the <term>bazaars</term> <note>marketplaces</note>: "Whoever wishes to plunder, go to the house of Ghanim, son of Ayyub!" <note>historical note: These plunderings were once sanctioned by custom. For example, in later generations, Turkish governors sometimes allowed soldiers to loot towns as a way to settle unpaid wages.</note> 

So the crowds flocked there, only to find that Ghanim's mother and sister had built a <term>cenotaph</term> <note>a monument erected in honor of a person whose body is elsewhere; used here as a place for the women to mourn</note> in the middle of the house and sat by it weeping for him. The mob seized the two women without explaining why and, after looting the house, brought them before the viceroy. He questioned them about Ghanim, and both replied, "We have had no news of him for a year or more." So the guards returned them to their home. 

This is the situation regarding them; but as for Ghanim, when he saw his wealth stolen and his ruin complete, he wept for himself until his heart nearly broke. Then he traveled on aimlessly until the end...

<header>The Tale of Ghanim bin Ayyub.</header>

As the day progressed, hunger weighed heavily on him and walking exhausted him. Upon coming to a village, he entered a mosque <note>The mosque served as a lodging for poor travelers, much as a chapel in Iceland might serve the wealthy. I have often taken advantage of the mosque for shelter, but as a rule it is unpleasant, as the matting is not only torn but infested with insects. Juvenal seems to allude to the Jewish Synagogue being used similarly: <note>original: "in quâ te quæro proseuchâ?"</note> "In which house of prayer shall I look for you?" (III. 296). Similarly, in Acts 3, we find the lame, blind, and helpless in the Temple porch.</note> where he sat down on a mat and leaned his back against the wall. However, he soon collapsed to the ground in an extremity of famine and fatigue. 

He lay there until dawn, his heart fluttering from lack of food. Because of his heavy sweating, lice <note>These foul insects were thought to be produced by perspiration. It is a milestone in a civilized traveler's life when he catches his first louse.</note> crawled over his skin; his breath became foul, and his entire physical condition was transformed. When the villagers arrived for the dawn prayer, they found him lying prostrate and sickly. He was thin from hunger, yet he still showed clear signs of his former wealth. 

As soon as prayers were over, they approached him. Understanding that he was starving and cold, they gave him an old robe with ragged sleeves and asked, "O stranger, where are you from and what sickness has overcome you?" 

He opened his eyes and wept but could not answer. Seeing that he was starving, one of them brought him a saucer of honey and two barley flatbreads. He ate a little, and they sat with him until sunrise, when they went to their work. He stayed with them in this state for a month as his sickness and weakness increased. The villagers wept for him and, pitying his condition, consulted one another about his case. They agreed to send him to the hospital in Baghdad. <note>The Muslim peasant is a kind-hearted person and will make many sacrifices for a sick stranger, even one of a different faith. It is a matter of a <term>point of honor</term> <note>original: "pundonor"</note> for the village.</note> 

In the meantime, two beggar-women—who were actually Ghanim's mother and sister <note>Such treatment of innocent women was far too common under the Caliphate and in contemporary Europe.</note>—entered the mosque. When he saw them, he gave them the bread that was by his head. They slept by his side that night, but he did not recognize them. 

The next day, the villagers brought a camel and said to the camel driver, "Place this sick man on your beast and carry him to Baghdad. Leave him at the hospital door. Perhaps he will be treated and healed there, and you shall have your payment." <note>This may also mean, "And Heaven will reward you," but camel drivers do not usually accept promises of future payment.</note> 

"To hear is to comply," said the man. So they brought...

Then she provided him with wine and medicines and sat by his head for a while. Afterward, she mounted her horse and returned to her palace, continuing to visit every bazaar in search of her lover. 

Meanwhile, Ghanim’s mother and his sister Fitnah arrived in Baghdad and met the Syndic. He brought them to Kut al-Kulub and said to her, “O Princess of charitable ladies, a woman and her daughter arrived in our city today. They are beautiful, and signs of noble breeding and dignity are evident in them, even though they are dressed in coarse sackcloth and each has a beggar's pouch hanging from her neck. Their eyes are full of tears and their hearts are heavy with sorrow. I have brought them to you so that you might give them refuge and rescue them from poverty.”

# The Tale of Ghanim bin Ayyub.

When the Caliph heard this, he turned to the eunuchs and said, “Bring Ghanim here to me.” So Ja’afar went to fetch him; but Kut al-Kulub went ahead of him and told Ghanim, “The Caliph has sent to fetch you before him,” and she instructed him to show a quick wit, a firm heart, and eloquent speech. Then she dressed him in a magnificent robe and gave him plenty of gold coins <term>dinars</term>, saying, “Be generous with your gifts to the Caliph’s household as you go in to see him.” 

Soon Ja’afar, mounted on his Nubian mule, arrived to fetch him; Ghanim stepped forward to welcome the Minister <term>Wazir</term> and, wishing him a long life, kissed the ground before him. Now the star of his good fortune had risen and shone brightly. Ja’afar took him, and the two traveled together until they entered the presence of the Commander of the Faithful. When Ghanim stood in the presence, he looked at the ministers, commanders <term>Emirs</term>, chamberlains, viceroys, grandees, and captains, and then at the Caliph. Thereupon, he spoke with great sweetness and eloquence and, bowing his head to the ground, broke out into these improvised verses:

> May that King’s life last a mighty span,
> Whose great generosity all his subjects witness.
> None other than he shall be called Caesar <term>Kaysar</term> <note>original: "Kaysar"</note>,
> Lord of a noble palace and a grand court <term>Divan</term>.
> Kings lay their jewels in the dust of his threshold
> As they bow and salute the powerful man;
> His very gaze overwhelms them and they all recoil,
> Bowing their faces to the ground with pale looks.
> Yet they benefit from his royal grace,
> And gain the status and rank of a high sultan <term>soldan</term>.
> The earth's plains are too small for your world of men;
> Set your camp in the highest heaven of Saturn <term>Kaywán</term>!<note>1</note>
> May the King of Kings always hold you dear;
> May you have wise counsel and a steady plan,
> Until your justice spreads over the wide world
> And those near and far are treated with equal fairness.

When he finished his improvisation, the Caliph was pleased by it and marveled at his eloquence and the sweetness of his speech—And Shahrazad noticed the dawn of day and stopped saying her permitted say.

### Now when it was the forty-fifth Night,

She said: It has come to my knowledge, O auspicious King, that the Caliph, after marveling at Ghanim’s eloquence and the sweetness of his speech, said to him, "Draw near to me." So he approached, and the King said, "Tell me your story and explain your circumstances." 

So Ghanim sat down and told him everything that had happened to him in Baghdad, from his sleeping in the tomb to his opening the chest after the three slaves had left. In short, he informed him of everything that had occurred from beginning to end—none of which we will repeat, for interest fades in twice-told tales. 

The Caliph was convinced that he was an honest man; so he bestowed upon him a robe of honor and placed him near himself as a sign of favor, saying to him, "Forgive me for any wrong I have done you." <note>original: "Acquit me of the responsibility I have incurred" — a popular phrase meaning "Pardon me if I injured thee."</note> 

Ghanim did so, saying, "O our lord the Sultan, truly your slave and everything his two hands possess belong to his master." 

The Caliph was pleased by this and gave orders to set aside a palace for him, assigning him a salary, allowances, rations, and gifts, all of which amounted to an immense sum. So Ghanim moved there with his sister and mother. After this, the Caliph heard that Ghanim’s sister, Fitnah, was such a beauty that she was a true "**fitnah**" <note>A "fitnah" is a seduction, a charmer, or a source of social discord. The double meaning has been noted previously.</note>—a total seduction—and he asked Ghanim for her hand in marriage. Ghanim replied, "She is your handmaid, just as I am your slave." 

The Caliph thanked him and gave him a hundred thousand gold coins <term>dinars</term>. He then summoned the witnesses and the judge <term>Kazi</term>, and on the very same day, they signed the two marriage contracts: one between the Caliph and Fitnah, and the other between Ghanim bin Ayyub and Kut al-Kulub. Both marriages were consummated on that same night. 

When morning came, the Caliph ordered that the history of everything that had happened to Ghanim from first to last be recorded and deposited in the royal archives, so that those who came after him might read it and marvel at the workings of Destiny and put their trust in Him who created the night and the day. ## TALE OF KING OMAR BIN AL-NU'UMAN AND HIS SONS SHARRKAN AND ZAU AL-MAKAN,
### AND THE STRANGE AND UNUSUAL THINGS THAT BEFELL THEM. <note>original: "and what befel them of things seld-seen and peregrine."</note>

THE King asked her, "And what was their story?" and she answered:—It has reached me, O auspicious King, that there was in the City of Peace, Baghdad, before the Caliphate of Abd al-Malik bin Marwan, <note>The fifth Umayyad Caliph, reigning from 65–86 A.H. (685–704 A.D.).</note> a King named Omar bin al-Nu'uman. He was one of the mighty giants and had conquered the Chosroes of Persia and the Caesars of Eastern Rome. No one could approach him when he was angry, <note>This does not merely mean that no one was safe from his wrath or could approach him in the heat of battle; it is a reference to the masterful "King Kulayb," who established game laws in his territory and would allow no man to approach his campfire. Furthermore, the Jinn lights a fire to lure travelers; but if his victim is brave enough to face him, the Jinn invites him to enjoy the warmth.</note> nor was any man able to face him on the battlefield. When he was enraged, sparks of flame came out of his nostrils. He had established himself as King over all corners of the earth, and Allah had made all His creatures subject to him; his word reached every great city, and his armies had raided the farthest lands. The East and the West had come under his command, along with all the regions that lay between them: India, Sindh, and China, <note>China.</note> the Holy Land, Al-Hijaz, the fertile mountains of Yemen, and the islands of India and China. Moreover, he <note>This knightly tale, the longest in the Nights (Nights 44–145), comprises about one-eighth of the whole work. It does not appear in the Breslau Edition. Lane, who finds it "objectionable," reduces it to just two of its episodes: Aziz and Azizah, and Taj al-Muluk. On the other hand, it has been published as a separate volume (8vo, 240 pages) titled "Sharrkan, an Arab Tale" translated by M. Asselan Riche, etc., Paris: Dondey-Dupré, 1829. It has its long passages and at times is tedious enough, but it is interesting as a comparison between the chivalry of Islam and European knight-errantry. Although all the characters are fictitious, the period is evidently set in the early Crusading days. Caesarea, the second capital of Palestine—captured during the Caliphate of Omar in 19 A.H. and later recovered—was fortified in 353 A.H. (963 A.D.) as a base against the Arabs by the Emperor Phocas (the Arabic "Nakfur," i.e., Nicephorus). In 498 A.H. (1104 A.D.), Crusader ships caused much damage by plundering merchant ships between Egypt and Syria, which is alluded to in this romance. However, the storyteller has not quite decided which Caesarea he is referring to, and M. Riche tells us that Caesarea is a "city in Mauritania, in Africa" <note>original: "ville de la Mauritanie, en Afrique"</note>.</note>

He reigned supreme over the northern lands and Diyar Bakr (Mesopotamia), over Sudan (the land of the Blacks in the East), the Islands of the Ocean, and all the world-famous rivers: the Sayhun, the Jayhun, <note>The Jaxartes and the Oxus (Bactrus) rivers, though these names were often used loosely.</note> the Nile, and the Euphrates. He sent envoys and ambassadors to the most remote capitals to bring him accurate reports. They would return with news of justice and peace, along with assurances of loyalty and obedience. Prayers were offered in the pulpits for King Omar bin al-Nu'uman, for he was—O Ruler of the Age—a truly noble King. From every land under his rule, he received rare gifts, tolls, and tribute.

This mighty monarch had a son named <term>Sharrkan</term>, <note>In full, "Sharrun kana," meaning "an evil (Sharr) has come into existence (kana)," or "bane to the foe." This is a pre-Islamic knightly name. The hero of the romance "Al-Dalhamah" is similarly described as a bitter gourd (colocynth), a viper, or a calamity.</note> who resembled his father more than any other man. He proved to be one of the wonders of his age, subduing the brave and bringing ruin and destruction to his rivals. Because of this, his father loved him with the greatest possible love and named him heir to the kingdom. This Prince grew until he reached manhood at twenty years of age, and Allah made his subjects submit to him because of his immense strength and skill in battle.

Now his father, King Omar, had four legal wives, but Allah had granted him no son by them except for Sharrkan, whom he had fathered with one of them; the others were barren. Additionally, he had three hundred and sixty concubines—one for each day of the Coptic year—who came from every nation. He provided a private chamber for each of them within his own palace. He had built twelve pavilions, one for each month, each containing thirty private rooms, totaling three hundred and sixty. There he housed his handmaidens, and according to law, he assigned each woman her specific night. He would sleep with her and not return to her for a full year. <note>This refers to Islamic law (see Quran chapter 4, which draws from the Talmud) stating a man should only marry if he can satisfy his wife. Furthermore, he must distribute his attention equally, and each wife has a right to her designated night unless she waives it. This applied even to the wives of the Prophet Muhammad; his biographies record instances where his wives gave up their nights to one another. M. Riche also describes the King's "spicy Frenchwoman" <note>original: "la piquante francaise"</note> (p. 15).</note> In this manner, he lived for a long time. Meanwhile, his son Sharrkan was becoming famous throughout the world. His father was proud of him as his strength continued to grow, until he surpassed...

<gloss>1</gloss> Similarly, the famous mosque in Istanbul, renowned for being the largest church in the world, is known to the Greeks as "Agia (pronounced Aya) Sophia" and to Muslims as "Aya Sofiyeh" (Holy Wisdom)—referring to the Logos or the Second Person of the Trinity (not a female saint). ## Tale of King Omar bin al-Nu’uman and his Sons

Their number was ten thousand horsemen, in addition to the infantry and camp followers. They loaded their baggage onto their pack animals; the war drums beat, the trumpets blared, and the banners and standards were unfurled. Sharrkan mounted his horse with the Vizier Dandan by his side, while the flags fluttered over their heads. The army set out and traveled continuously, with the Ambassadors leading the way, until the day ended and night approached; then they halted and encamped for the night. As soon as God brought the dawn, they mounted and hastened on, guided by the Ambassadors, for twenty days. By the night of the twenty-first day, they reached a fine, spacious valley <term>original: "Wady"</term> filled with trees and shrubbery. Sharrkan ordered them to stop there and commanded a three-day halt. They dismounted and pitched their tents, spreading their camp across the right and left slopes of the extensive valley, while the Vizier Dandan and King Afridun’s Ambassadors pitched their tents in the center of the valley floor <note>Travelers often prefer such sites because they are sheltered from the wind and the ground is soft for pitching tents; however, many have come to grief from sudden flash floods following rain.</note>.

As for Sharrkan, he stayed behind for a while until everyone had dismounted and dispersed across the valley sides. He then slackened the reins of his horse, intending to explore the valley and stand guard personally, following his father’s instructions and because they were on the frontier of Greece <note>original: "Græcia-land"</note> and in enemy territory. He rode out alone after ordering his armed slaves and bodyguard to camp near the Vizier Dandan. He traveled along the side of the valley until a quarter of the night had passed. At that point, he felt tired and drowsiness overcame him, so much so that he could no longer urge his horse forward with his heels. He was accustomed to resting on horseback; so, when sleep overpowered him, he drifted off. The horse continued walking with him until half the night had passed and entered a thicket <note>Arabic: "Ghábah." Not a forest in the Western sense, but a place where water collects and trees (mostly mimosas), which are elsewhere widely scattered, form a dense growth. These are favorite places for wild animals during the noon heat.</note> which was overgrown with vegetation. Sharrkan did not wake up until his horse stumbled on the wooded ground. He started awake and found himself among the trees. The moon had risen and shone brightly over both horizons, East and West. He was startled to find himself alone in this place and said—

The "dirty water" refers to semen. The physiological ideas of the Koran are specific: it suggests that the male semen is in the loins and that of women in the breastbone (Chapter 86); that the mingled seed of the two (Chapter 76) fertilizes the ovary and that the child is fed through the navel with menstrual blood, which is why menstruation stops during pregnancy. Barzoi (from the book *Kalilah and Dimnah*) says: "Man's seed, falling into the woman's womb, is mixed with her seed and her blood; when it thickens and curdles the Spirit moves it and it turns about like liquid cheese; then it solidifies, its arteries are formed, its limbs constructed and its joints distinguished. There is also an early version of the "spermatozoa theory." We read in the Koran (Chapter 7), "Your Lord drew forth their descendants from the loins of the sons of Adam." Commentators say that Allah stroked Adam's back and extracted from his loins all his descendants who would ever exist, in the shape of small ants; these spirits admitted their dependence on God and were dismissed to return from where they came. This shows that the doctrine of pre-existence is known to Muslims; there is some similarity between it and the modern theory of *generatio ex animalculis in semine marium* <note>original: "generation from tiny animals in the male seed"</note>. "By God, my lady," said Sharrkan (who was now very angry with her), "if I were Master al-Safdi, Master Mohammed Kimal, or Ibn al-Saddi² in their prime, I would not have even noticed these maneuvers you mention. For my mistress, by God, you did not throw me to the ground by your strength, but by the charms of your body; we men of Mesopotamia so love a well-formed thigh that I lost both my senses and my foresight. But now, if you wish, you shall try a third round with me while I have my wits about me. This last match is allowed to me by the rules of the game, which say 'the best of three'; furthermore, I have regained my focus." 

When she heard his words, she said to him, "Haven't you had your fill of this wrestling, you defeated man? However, come on if you wish; but know that this must be the final round." 

Then she leaned forward and challenged him, and Sharrkan did the same, setting to it in real earnest and being very cautious about the throw. The two struggled for a while, and the young woman found a strength in him she had not observed before and said to him, "O Muslim, you are now on your mettle." 

"Yes," he replied, "you know that I have only this one round left, after which each of us will go a different way." 

She laughed and he laughed too;³ then she reached for his thigh and caught a firm hold of it by surprise, which made him hit the ground and fall flat on his back. She laughed at him and said, "Are you an eater of bran? You are like a Bedouin’s cap which falls off with every touch, or else the 'Father of Winds'⁴ that drops before a puff of air. Shame on you, you poor thing!" She added, "Go back to the Muslim army and send us someone other than—"

<sup>1</sup> <note>Kuthayyir ibn Abi Jumah was a poet and a famous *Rawi* (tale-reciter) mentioned by Ibn Khallikan. He lived in Medina and sang of the charms of a woman named Azzah, leading to his nickname *Sahib* (lover or companion) of Azzah. Since he died in 726 AD (A.H. 105), his presence here is a significant historical mistake (anachronism); the fictional Sharrkan is set in an earlier period, before the reign of Caliph Abd al-Malik bin Marwan (685–705 AD).</note>
<sup>2</sup> <note>Jamil bin Ma'amar was a poet and lover who lived at the same time as Al-Kuthayyir.</note>

Then she rose and went to her bedroom and slept, while Sharrkan slept in his place until morning dawned. He plucked the fruits of her necklace in competition, ◦ And the pearls of her breast that lie in a gold mine.
Her brow is like pure water on bars of silver, ◦ And her cheeks show roses that compete with rubies;
It seems to me that in her eyes, the violet's hue ◦ Lies set in deep purple from the *Ithmid's*² dye.

---

¹ Arabic: "Tafazzal," a word frequently used in conversation meaning "favor me," "please," etc.
² The word has a long history. From the Greek *stimmi* or *stibi* <note>original: "στίμμι" or "στίβι"</note> comes the Latin *stibium* ; while the Low-Latin *antimonium* and the Spanish *Althimod* are formed by rearranging the letters <term>metathesis: the transposition of sounds or letters in a word</term> for *Al-Ithmid*. Dictionaries define the substance as a stone from which antimony is prepared; but the Arabs understand it as a semi-mythical mineral of yellow color which enters the veins of the eyes and gives them lynx-like vision. The famous Anz, nicknamed *Zarká* (the blue-eyed) of the Yamámah province, used it; and, according to some, she invented *Kohl* <term>Kohl: a traditional eye cosmetic</term>. When her ancient tribe, the Jadis, had destroyed all of the rival race of Tasm except for Ribáh ibn Murrah, the sole survivor fled to the King of Yemen <note>original: "Tobba of Al-Yaman"</note>, who sent an army to avenge him. The king commanded his soldiers <term>Himyarites: people of the ancient kingdom of Himyar in Yemen</term> to cut tree branches and use them as screens (similar to the "Birnam Wood" from Macbeth). Zarká, from her watchtower <term>Utum: a square, stone tower or castle</term>, saw the army from three days' march away and cried, "O people, either trees or the Himyarites are coming upon you!" adding, in *Rajaz* verse <term>Rajaz: a specific meter in Arabic poetry</term>:

> I swear by God <note>original: "Allah"</note> that trees are crawling forward, or that the Himyarites are carrying something they are dragging along!

She then saw a man repairing his sandal. But the Jadis people disbelieved her; like Cassandra <note>Cassandra: a figure from Greek myth who foretold the truth but was never believed</note>, she was killed.

See C. de Perceval i. 101; Arab. Prov. i. 192; and Chenery (p. 381. The Assemblies of Al-Hariri; London, Williams and Norgate, 1867). I have made many inquiries into the true nature of *Ithmid* and failed to learn anything specific: on the Upper Nile, the word is equivalent to Kohl.

¹ The general color of chessmen in the East, where the game is played on a cloth more often than a board.
² Arabic “Al-fíl,” the elephant = the French *fol* or *fou* and our bishop. I have derived “elephant” from *Píl* (old Persian and Sanskrit *Pilu*) and Arabic *Fíl*, with the article *Al-Fíl*, which led to the Greek *ἐλέφας* <note>original: "elephas" — elephant</note>. The grain is spread over a round, smooth floor of dried mud in the open air and threshed using various methods. In Egypt, the favorite is a chair-like machine called a *Norag*, which runs on iron plates and is drawn by bulls or cows over the corn. Generally, however, Muslims prefer the old classical *Tribulum* (Latin), a slipper-shaped wooden sled with a base covered in large-headed iron nails or sharp fragments of flint or basalt. ² <note>The Farsakh (German *Stunde*) is a measure of time rather than distance; it is an hour's travel or its equivalent, a league, a mile = three English statute miles. The word is still used in Persia, its true home, but not elsewhere. It is very ancient, having been defined as a linear measure of distance by Herodotus (ii. 5 and 6; v. 53), who calculates it at 30 furlongs (furrow-lengths, 8 to the statute mile). But now I ask of your favor that you make me a present of the jewel which he gave you, if you have accepted it." 

"I hear and obey," replied Sharrkan, and he gave it to her. 

Then she said, "Fear nothing," and talked with him for a while, continuing, "I fear lest my father hear that I am with you and will not sit idly by my loss, but will try his best to find me. To that end, he may ally himself with King Afridun on account of his daughter Sophia, and both may come against you with armies, and so great turmoil may occur." 

When Sharrkan heard these words, he said to her, "O my lady, if it pleases you to stay with us, do not worry about them; even if all those on land and sea gathered together against us." 

"It is well," she rejoined; "if you treat me well, I will stay with you, and if you deal badly with me, I will depart from you." Then she ordered her slave-maidens to bring food; so they set the tables, and Sharrkan ate a little and went away to his own house, feeling troubled and perturbed. 

That was his situation; but regarding the affairs of his father, Omar bin al-Nu'uman: after dismissing his son Sharrkan, he arose and, taking the other two jewels, went to the Lady Sophia. She stood up when she saw him and remained standing until he was seated. Presently, his two children, Zau al-Makan and Nuzhat al-Zaman, came to him. He kissed them and hung a jewel around each one’s neck, at which they rejoiced and kissed his hands. 

Then they went to their mother, who rejoiced in their joy and wished the King a long life. So he asked her, "Why have you not informed me all this time that you are the daughter of King Afridun, Lord of Constantinople, so that I might have honored you still more, increased your dignity, and raised your rank?" 

"O King," answered Sophia, "what could I desire greater or higher than my current standing with you, overwhelmed as I am with your favors and your benefits? And, furthermore, God <note>original: "Allah"</note> has blessed me with two children by you, a son and a daughter."

### Now when it was the Fifty-second Night,

She said: I have heard, O fortunate King, that Princess Abrizah said to the slave Al-Ghazban, “Is this all that remains for me—to surrender to a slave after having refused kings and heroes?” She was furious with him and cried out, “Woe to you! What are you saying? Shame on you! Do not talk like this in my presence. Know that I will never consent to what you say, even if I must drink the cup of death. Wait until I have given birth and delivered the afterbirth, and then, if you are able, do with me as you will. But if you do not stop this indecent talk right now, I will surely kill myself with my own hand, leave this world, and be at peace from all this.” Then she began to recite spontaneously <term>extempore</term>¹: ——

> O spare me, Ghazban, for I have already suffered enough ◦ from the heavy blows of fate, misfortune, and misery!
> Adultery my Lord forbids to all humanity; ◦ He said, “Whoever breaks my command shall find their home in Hell!”

### Now when it was the **Fifty-third Night**,

She said: It has reached me, O auspicious King, that when the sages and the scholars stood in the presence of King Hardub, he honored them with great distinction and entrusted the handmaidens to them, commanding that they be instructed in all types of knowledge, philosophy, and courtly etiquette. The scholars set themselves to do his bidding.

Such was the case with King Hardub; but as for King Omar bin al-Nu'man, when he returned from his sport and hunting and entered his palace, he looked for Princess Abrizah but could not find her. No one knew where she was, nor could anyone give him news of her. This was distressing to him, and he said, "How could the lady leave the palace without anyone knowing? Had my kingdom been at stake in this situation, it would be in a dangerous state since there is no one to govern it! I will never again go out for sport and hunting until I have stationed guards at the gates who will keep a strict watch over them!"

He was deeply vexed and his heart was troubled by the loss of Princess Abrizah. At this point, his son Sharrkan returned from his journey; his father told him what had happened and informed him how the lady had fled while he was out hunting, which caused Sharrkan to grieve with exceeding grief.

Then King Omar began visiting his children every day and doting on them; he brought in learned men and scholars to teach them, providing them with stipends. When Sharrkan saw this, he flew into a great rage and became envious of his brother and sister until the signs of frustration appeared on his face. He continued to grow weak and sickly because of this matter, so one day his father said to him, "Why do I see you grown so weak in body and pale of face?"

"O my father," Sharrkan replied...

"Every time I see you fondle my brother and sister and make a fuss over them, jealousy seizes me. I fear it will grow within me until I kill them, and you kill me in return. This Prince had reached the age of fourteen and occupied himself with piety and prayers, loving the poor, the <term>Olema</term> <note>a body of Muslim scholars recognized as having specialized knowledge of Islamic sacred law and theology</note>, and the students of the Koran, so that all the people of Baghdad, both men and women, loved him. And when he had finished his verses, they wept, and the stoker said to him, "O my son, we hardly believed that you had recovered; <note>That is, "You have only just recovered."</note> so take heart and do not weep, for I fear you might have a relapse." > Gather provisions in this world before you go upon your way; * And know how surely Death descends to ambush your destiny:
> All your worldly goods are but pride and the most painful regret; * All your worldly life is the troubling of your soul in empty show:
> Tell me, is not this earthly home like a traveler's resting place, * Where at night he makes his camels kneel <note>The original text uses the term "nakhs." To "Nakh" is to make a guttural "Ikh! Ikh!" sound until the camel kneels. This explains the name of the "Barr al-Manakhah" (the place of kneeling) in Medina. There is a specific camel-vocabulary used by Arabs, similar to "Gee-up," made of shortened words.</note> and moves off at the break of day?

And he continued to weep and wail over his separation; meanwhile, the stoker also wept for the loss of his wife, yet he did not cease to comfort Zau al-Makan until morning dawned. "Yes," replied Zau al-Makan, "and I can no longer stay here; so I will entrust you to God's care and set out with these people and journey with them, bit by bit, until I come to my homeland." The stoker said, "And I will go with you; for in truth I cannot bear to part with you. I have done you a kindness in serving you, and I mean to complete it by tending to you on your travels." At this, Zau al-Makan rejoiced and said, "May God abundantly reward you for my sake!" and he was pleased with the idea of them traveling together. The stoker at once went out and bought another—

---

The hot land <note>original: "tierra caliente"</note> is the coastal region of Al-Hijaz, the Muslims' Holy Land. Its “Arabah,” a very small tract that gave its name to a very large region, must not be confused—as some have done—with the Wady Arabah, the ancient outlet of the Dead Sea. The derivation of “Arab” from “Ya’arab,” a fictional son of Joktan, is mythological. In Hebrew, *Arabia* may be called “Eretz Ereb” (or “Arab”), meaning “Land of the West” <note>original: "Eretz Ereb"</note>; but in Arabic, “Gharb” <note>original: "Gharb"</note> is the word for the West <note>original: "the Occident"</note>, and the Arab people existed long before the Hebrews.

He walked on ahead of her, and when she followed him, he signaled to his men to go on in advance to harness the camels <term>dromedaries</term>, load them with their packs, and prepare water and provisions, so they would be ready to set out as soon as he arrived with the girl. Now this Bedouin <term>Badawi</term> was a low-born peasant, a highway robber and a traitor even to his dearest <term>lief</term> friend; he was a thorough rogue, a master of plots and trickery <term>chicane</term>. He had neither daughter nor son and was only passing through the town when, by the decree of God <term>the Decreer</term>, he encountered this unfortunate woman. 

He did not stop talking with her along the road until they had gone beyond the city of Jerusalem. Once outside, he joined his companions and found they had prepared the camels. The Bedouin mounted a camel and seated Nuzhat al-Zaman behind him, and they rode all through the night. Then she realized that the Bedouin's proposal was a trap and that he had tricked her; she continued weeping and crying out the whole night long as they journeyed toward the mountains, fearing that anyone might see them. 

When it was near dawn, they dismounted from their camels and the Bedouin came up to Nuzhat al-Zaman and said to her, "You city harlot, why are you weeping? By Allah, if you do not keep quiet, I will beat you to death, you city trash!" 

When she heard this, she loathed her life and longed for death. She turned to him and said, "You accursed old man, you graybeard of hell, how could I have trusted you? You have betrayed me, and now you want to torture me?" 

When he heard her reply, he cried out, "You lazy hussy, do you dare to argue with me?" He stood over her and beat her with a whip, saying, "If you do not hold your peace, I will kill you!" 

So she was silent for a while, but then she remembered her brother and the happy life she had once known, and she shed tears in secret. The next day, she turned to the Bedouin and said to him, "How could you play this trick on me and lure me into these barren and rocky mountains? What is your plan for me?" 

When he heard her words, he hardened his heart and said to her, "You lazy, unlucky, and insolent girl! Will you argue with me again?" He took the whip and struck her on the back until she felt faint. Then she bowed down over his feet and kissed¹ them, and he stopped beating her.

¹ The *Tartur* was a specific turban worn by the Northern Arabs and shown in old prints. In modern Egypt, the term is applied to the tall, sugar-loaf felt caps worn mostly by regular Dervishes. Burckhardt (Proverbs 194 and 398) describes it as the high cap of felt or fur belonging to the irregular cavalry called *Dely* or *Delaty*. In Darfur, “Tartur” is a conical cap adorned with beads and shells <term>cowries</term> worn by the *Manghwah* or buffoon, who corresponds with the Egyptian “Khalbús” or “Maskharah” <note>clown or jester</note> and the Turkish “Sutari.” For an illustration, see Plate iv. figure 10 of *Voyage au Darfour* by Mohammed El-Tounsy (The Tunisian), Paris, Duprat, 1845.

### Now when it was the Six-and-Fiftieth Night,

She said: It has reached me, O auspicious King, that when the Bedouin <term>Badawi</term> gave the barley scone to Nuzhat al-Zaman and promised he would sell her to a good man like himself, she replied, “Whatever you do is right!” Around midnight, when hunger gnawed at her, <note>The original text says "hunger burned her," which the translator notes is a picturesque phrase.</note> she ate a very little of that barley bread. Then the Bedouin ordered his party to set out; they loaded their gear, and he mounted a camel, placing Nuzhat al-Zaman behind him. 

They traveled without stopping for three days until they entered the city of Damascus and stayed at the Sultan’s Inn <term>Khan</term>, right next to the Viceroy’s Gate. By then, she had lost her color from grief and the exhaustion of such travel, and she did not stop weeping over her misfortunes. 

The Bedouin came up to her and said, “You city filth! By the honor of my cap, if you don't stop this crying, I will sell you to no one but a Jew!” Then he stood up, took her by the hand, and led her to a room. He walked off to the bazaar <note>Marketplace</note> and went to the merchants who dealt in female slaves. He began to negotiate with them, saying, “I have brought a female slave whose brother fell ill. I sent him to my people near Jerusalem so they might care for him until he is cured. As for her, I want to sell her; however, after that dog of a brother fell sick, the separation from him was very painful for her. Since then, she does nothing but weep. Now, I hope that whoever intends to buy her from me will speak gently to her and say, ‘Your brother is with me in Jerusalem, ill.’ If you do this, I will be flexible regarding her price.” 

Then one of the merchants approached him and asked, “How old is she?” 

He answered, “She is a virgin who has just reached marriageable age. She is gifted with intelligence, good breeding, wit, beauty, and loveliness. But since the day I sent her brother to Jerusalem, her heart has been yearning for him, so much so that her beauty has faded and her value has decreased.” 

When the merchant heard this, he set out with the Bedouin and said, “O Chief <term>Shaykh</term> <note>The original note defines this as an Elder or Chief, noting it was becoming a common term in English and citing Abraham as the first "Shaykh."</note> of the Arabs, I will go with you and buy this girl from you, whom you praise so highly for her wit, manners, beauty, and loveliness. I will pay you her price..."

She said: It has reached me, O auspicious King, that when the merchant saved Nuzhat al-Zaman from the Bedouin <term>Badawi</term> and took her to his lodgings, he dressed her in the finest clothing. The merchant replied, “I bought her for one hundred thousand dinars, and her clothes cost me another hundred thousand.”

Thereupon, the Sultan summoned the four judges <term>Kazi: a judge in a Muslim legal system</term> and paid the merchant the money in their presence. Then he said, “I call you to witness that I free this, my slave-girl, and intend to marry her.” 

So the judges wrote out the deed of emancipation and the marriage contract, and then the Sultan scattered much gold over the heads of those present. The pages and the eunuchs gathered up this generous gift <term>largesse: money or gifts given freely and generously</term>. Then, after paying the merchant his money, Sharrkan ordered them to write a perpetual decree for him, exempting him from tolls, taxes, or duties upon his merchandise and forbidding anyone in his entire government from bothering him. Finally, he gave the merchant a magnificent robe of honor.

# Alf Laylah wa Laylah.

...the women with her on one side, and King Sharrkan, the four judges <term>Kazi: a judge in an Islamic legal system</term>, and the merchant seated beside him on the other. Presently, King Sharrkan called to her and said, “O Queen, the glory of your age, this merchant has described you as being learned and accomplished. He claims that you are skilled in all branches of knowledge, even in astrology. So, let us hear something of all that he has mentioned, and favor us with a short discourse on such subjects.” She replied, saying, “O King, to hear is to obey. <note>original: "Sam'an wa Ta'atan"</note> 

The first subjects I will discuss are the art of government and the duties of Kings, what is required of those who administer the law according to religious principles, and what is expected of them regarding proper speech and conduct. Know then, O King, that all human works lead either to a religious or a secular life. No one achieves a religious life except through this world, because the world is the best path to the afterlife. 

Now, the affairs of this world are only kept in order by the actions of its people, and human activities are divided into four categories: government, commerce, agriculture, and craftsmanship. 

Government requires perfect administration with just and true judgment, for government is the pivot of the world's structure—and this world is the path to the afterlife. Allah Almighty made the world for His servants as travel provisions <term>viaticum: a supply of food or money for a journey</term> for the traveler to reach their goal. It is fitting for each person to take only as much as will bring them to God, and that they do not follow their own whims or individual lusts in this matter. 

If people would take worldly goods with justice and equity, all causes of conflict would be eliminated. However, they take things by force and according to their own desires, and their persistence in this behavior gives rise to conflict. Therefore, they have need of a ruler <term>Sultan: a sovereign or king</term> to provide justice between them and order their affairs. If the King does not restrain his people from harming one another, the strong will drive the weak to the wall. 

Hence, Ardeshir <note>Ardeshir I (Artaxerxes), the founder of the Sassanid Empire.</note> says, 'Religion and Kingship are twins; religion is a hidden treasure and the King is its keeper.' Both Divine Laws and human intelligence indicate that it is necessary for the people to adopt a ruler who shall protect the oppressed from the oppressor and give the weak justice against the strong, and...

# Tale of King Omar bin al-Nu'uman and his Sons.

...to restrain the violence of the proud and those who rebel against authority. For know, O King, that the character of the times is determined by the character of the Sultan. As the Apostle of Allah <note>The Prophet Muhammad</note> (peace and salvation be upon him!) said: "There are two classes of people who, if they are good, the people will be good; and if they are bad, the people will be bad: the scholars <term>Ulama: religious and legal scholars</term> and the leaders <term>Emirs: commanders or princes</term>." 

It was also said by a certain sage: "There are three kinds of Kings: the King of Faith, the King who protects what is sacred, and the King of his own desires." 

The King of Faith compels his subjects to follow their religion, and it is necessary that he be the most devout of all <note>This refers to the proverb "The people follow the religion of their King," or in Latin, *Cujus regio, ejus religio* (Whose realm, his religion).</note>, for he is the model they follow in matters of faith. It is the duty of the people to obey him in whatever he commands according to Divine Law. He must hold those who are dissatisfied in the same regard as those who are content, out of submission to the decrees of destiny. 

As for the King who protects what is sacred, he upholds both the affairs of religion and the world. He compels his people to follow Divine Law and to respect human rights. It is appropriate for him to master both the Pen and the Sword; for if anyone strays from what the Pen has written and their feet slip, the King shall correct their error with the sharp Sword and spread his justice over all mankind. 

As for the King of his own desires, he has no religion other than following his own whims. Since he does not fear the wrath of his Lord who placed him on the throne, his kingdom is destined for downfall, and his pride will end in the house of perdition <term>house of perdition: a state of eternal ruin or Hell</term>. 

Sages say: "The King needs many people, but the people need only one King." Therefore, it is proper that he be well-acquainted with their natures, so that he may turn their discord into harmony, surround them all with his justice, and overwhelm them with his generosity. 

Know, O King, that Ardeshir, called *Jamr Shadid* <note>original: "Jamr Shadíd" meaning "The Intense Coal"</note>, the third of the Kings of Persia, conquered the whole world and divided it into four regions. For this purpose, he commissioned four signet rings, one for each region. 

The first seal was for the sea and the regulation of prohibitions, and on it was written: **Alternatives**. 

The second was the seal of tribute and the collection of taxes, and on it was written: **Building up**. 

The third was the seal of the food supply department, and on it was written: **Plenty**. 

The fourth was the seal of the oppressed, and on it was written:

### Now when the Sixty-first Night arrived,

She said: It has reached me, O auspicious King, that Chosroes wrote to his son: "Do not be too lavish with your troops, or they will be too wealthy to need you; nor be stingy with them, or they will complain against you. Give your gifts deliberately and grant your favors wisely; be generous to them in times of success and do not neglect them in times of distress." 

There is a legend that a desert Arab once came to the Caliph Al-Mansur <note>The second Abbasid Caliph, ruled 754-775 AD.</note> and said, "Starve your dog and he will follow you." When the Caliph heard these words, he was angry with the Arab, but Abu l-Abbas of Tus said to him, "I fear that if someone other than you were to show him a piece of bread, the dog would follow him instead and leave you alone." At this, the Caliph Al-Mansur’s anger cooled. He realized that the desert Arab had intended no offense and ordered that a gift be given to him. 

And know, O King, that Abd al-Malik bin Marwan wrote to his brother Abd al-Aziz when he sent him to govern Egypt: "Pay close attention to your Secretaries and your Chamberlains. The Secretaries will keep you informed of established government matters, and the Chamberlains will guide you in matters of official ceremony, while your spending will make your troops known to you." 

Omar bin Al-Khattab <note>The famous companion of Muhammad who succeeded Abu Bakr as Caliph (634-644 AD). Sunnis know him as "Al-Adil," or "The Just," while Shias resent him for his rise to power and his perceived harshness. It is said he laughed once and wept once. He laughed when remembering how he once ate his idols made of dough during the pre-Islamic era of "The Ignorance." He wept when remembering how he buried his infant daughter alive; as he dug the grave, she patted the dust off his hair and beard. Omar was undoubtedly a significant figure, but he is often seen as a stern and unyielding leader, similar to a very strict and narrow-minded religious zealot. It is understandable why many Persians historically viewed him with such strong dislike.</note> (may Allah accept him!), when hiring a servant, used to set four conditions: first, that the servant should not ride the pack animals; second, that he should not wear expensive clothes; third, that he should not eat from the spoils of war; and fourth...

# Tale of King Omar bin al-Nu'uman and his Sons.

Fourth, that he should not put off praying until after the proper time. It is said that no wealth is more profitable than understanding, and there is no understanding like common sense and prudence, and there is no prudence like piety. There is no means of drawing near to God like good morals, no measure like good breeding, no trade like good works, and no profit like earning Divine favor. There is no temperance like staying within the limits of the law, no science like that of meditation, no worship like obeying the Divine commands, no faith like modesty, no calculation like humility, and no honor like knowledge. So guard the head and what it contains, and the belly and what it comprises; and think of death and judgment before they arrive. 

Ali (may Allah honor him!) says: "Beware of the wickedness of women and be on your guard against them. Do not consult them in anything;<note>¹ The austere Caliph Omar, whose whip was more feared than the sword, was the author of the celebrated saying: 'Consult women and do the exact opposite.' This saying is illustrated by many anecdotes known throughout the East.</note> but do not withhold kindness from them, lest they develop a hunger for intrigue." And he also said that whoever leaves the path of moderation will find his wits become confused; there are rules for this which we will mention, if it is Allah's will. 

And Omar (may Allah accept him!) says there are three kinds of women: first, the true believer who fears Heaven, is full of love and is fertile—she helps her partner against fate, rather than helping fate against her partner; second, the woman who loves only her children and nothing else; and lastly, she who is a shackle that Allah places on the neck of whomever He wills. 

Men are also of three kinds: the wise man, who exercises his own judgment; the wiser man, who—when something happens where he does not know the outcome—seeks people of good counsel and acts on their advice; and the unwise, indecisive man, who ignores the right way and pays no attention to those who would guide him straight. 

Justice is indispensable in all things; even slave girls have need of justice. People cite the example of highway robbers who live by violating humanity; if they did not deal fairly among themselves and observe justice in dividing their loot, their organization would fall apart.<note>² This is similar to our saying, "honor among thieves."</note> In short, the chief of all noble qualities is beneficence combined with benevolence; and how excellent is the saying of the poet:

> Through generosity and compassion, the youth rose to command his tribe;
> ->Go and do likewise, for it would be an easy task for you.<-

"...because there are seventy-two virtues in it, and perform the *Ghusl* <term>full ritual bath</term> on Friday as an atonement for everything that happened between the two Fridays." — And Shahrazad saw the break of day and stopped speaking.

### Now when it was the Sixty-second Night,

She said: I have heard, O fortunate King, that Ahnaf bin Qays replied to Mu'awiyah's <note>original: "Al-Mu'awiyah"</note> question, "And always use the tooth-stick <term>miswak</term>, because there are seventy-two virtues in it, and perform the complete Friday ablution as an atonement for everything between the two Fridays."

Mu'awiyah asked, "What is the advice you give to yourself?" 

"To plant my feet firmly on the ground, to move them deliberately, and to watch over them with my own eyes!"

"How do you behave when you visit someone who is not among the nobles of your tribe?"

"I lower my eyes modestly and I am the first to offer a greeting; I avoid what does not concern me and I am careful with my words!"

"And how do you act when you visit your equals?"

"I listen to them when they speak, and I do not attack them when they make a mistake!"

"When you visit your leaders?"

"I greet them without making any distracting signs and await their reply; if they tell me to draw near, I draw near; and if they pull away from me, I withdraw!"

"How do you behave with your wife?"

Ahnaf said, "Forgive me from answering this, O Commander of the Faithful!" 

But Mu'awiyah cried, "I urge you to tell me." 

He said, "I treat her kindly and show her affection, and I am generous in spending money on her, for womankind was created from a crooked rib." <note>The saying is attributed to Abraham when he was troubled by the difficult temper of Sarah: "Woman is made hard and crooked like a rib"; the modern addition is, "whoever would try to straighten her will break her."</note> 

"And how do you act when you intend to sleep with her?"

"I tell her to perfume herself and I kiss her until she is moved to desire; then, if things proceed as you know, <note>That is, "When ready and aroused."</note> I lay her on her back. If the seed remains in her womb, I say: 'O Allah, make it blessed and do not let it be wasted, but fashion it in the best of forms!' <note>"And perform first (before going in to your wives) some act which may be profitable to your souls"—or, for your soul's good. Without stopping, and in the same manner, Yezid and the Marwan family—such as Abd al-Malik, Walid, and Sulayman <note>The second, fifth, sixth, and seventh Umayyad Caliphs.</note>—drew water away from the stream until the main course dried up. <margin>Abu Bakr was originally named Abd al-Ka’bah (servant of the Ka'bah). He took the name Abdullah and was given the title Abu Bakr (father of the virgin) when Muhammad—who had previously married only widows—married his daughter, the famous (or infamous) Aisha. "Bikr" is the usual form, but "Bakr," which primarily means a young camel, is metaphorically applied to human youth. The first Caliph was a cloth merchant, like many of the Meccan chiefs. He is described as having a very fair complexion, a prominent brow, deep-set eyes, thin cheeks, a slender build, and lean hips; he stooped and had very little flesh on the backs of his hands. He used henna and *katam* <note>A plant used with henna to dye hair black</note> to dye his beard. The Persians, who hate him, call him "*Pir-i-Kaftar*" <note>original: "Pir-i-Kaftár"; literally "the old she-hyena"</note>, and believe that he wanders the deserts of Arabia in a state of perpetual rut that must be satisfied by males.</margin>

...that I was present, just as you were, when one of the descendants of Marwan <note>The Marwanids were a branch of the Umayyad dynasty.</note> was buried. There are many examples of this kind. One of the men in authority said: “I used to milk ewes during the Caliphate of Omar bin Abd al-Aziz, and one day I met a shepherd whose sheep were among a wolf or wolves. I thought they were dogs, for I had never seen wolves before. So I asked, ‘What are you doing with these dogs?’ The shepherd answered, ‘They are not dogs, but wolves.’ I asked, ‘Can wolves be with sheep and not hurt them?’ He replied, ‘When the head is healthy, the body is healthy.’” <note>The Turkish proverb says: "The fish begins to stink at the head."</note>

Omar bin Abd al-Aziz once preached from a pulpit of clay and, after praising and glorifying Allah Almighty, spoke these words: “O people, purify your innermost hearts so that your outward lives may be pure to your brothers, and abstain from the things of this world. Know that between us and Adam, there is not a single living man among the dead. Abd al-Malik and those who preceded him are dead; Omar shall also die, as will those who came before him.” 

Maslamah asked, “O Commander of the Faithful, if we place a pillow behind you, will you lean on it for a little while?”

She began to pour water on him, weeping until he regained consciousness. Seeing her in tears, he said to her, “What makes you weep, O Fatimah?” 

She replied, “O Commander of the Faithful, I saw you lying prostrate before us and thought of your prostration in death before Almighty Allah, and of your departure from the world...”

<note>
The "Greater Pilgrimage" occurs when the "Day of Arafat" (9th of Dhu al-Hijjah) falls upon a Friday. For more on this *Hajj al-Akbar*, see my *Pilgrimage* iii. 226. It is often confused by writers (even by the learned M. Caussin de Perceval) with the common Pilgrimage as opposed to the *Umrah*, or "Lesser Pilgrimage." The latter literally means living with a woman in her father’s house as opposed to *Ars*, or leading her to the husband’s home. It is applied to visiting Mecca and performing all the pilgrim rites, but not during the official Pilgrimage season. Hence its title *Hajj al-Asghar*, the "Lesser Hajj." However, "*Umrah*" is also applied to a certain ceremony between the hills of Safa (a large hard rock) and Marwah (a stone full of flints), which accompanies the Hajj and which I have described elsewhere. At Mecca, I also heard of two places called Al-Umrah: the Greater in the Fatima Valley and the Lesser, which is halfway closer to the city.
</note>

The text also provides a scholarly explanation of the distinctions between the Greater and Lesser Pilgrimages (Hajj and Umrah).</summary>

"Tell me the reason you left your father and how you came to be sold as a slave." When Sharrkan heard this, he was certain that she was his sister on his father's side <term>sword-side</term> and said to himself, "How can I have my sister as a wife? By God, I must marry her to one of my chamberlains; and if the matter becomes known, I will declare that I divorced her before the marriage was consummated and then married her to my Chief Chamberlain." Then he raised his head and, sighing, said, "O Nuzhat al-Zaman, you are truly my sister, and I cry out: I seek refuge with God from this sin into which we have fallen, for I am Sharrkan, son of Omar bin al-Nu'uman." She looked at him and knew he spoke the truth; and, becoming like one who had lost her mind, she wept and beat her face, exclaiming,

> "There is no power and there is no might except in God! Truly, we have fallen into a mortal sin!¹

What shall I do, and what shall I say to my father and my mother when they ask me, 'Where did you get your daughter?'" Sharrkan said, "It would be best for me to marry you to my Chamberlain and let you raise my daughter in his house, so that no one may know you are my sister. This has happened to us by the will of Almighty God for a purpose of His own, and nothing shall protect us except your marriage to this Chamberlain before anyone finds out." Then he began to comfort her and kiss her head, and she asked him, "What will you name the girl?" "Call her <term>Kuzia-Fakán</term>,"² he answered. Then he gave the mother in marriage to the Chief Chamberlain and moved her to his house with the child, whom they raised in the care of the slave-girls, feeding her with milk and medicine. ### Now when it was the Seventy-first Night,

She said: I have heard, O fortunate King, that they stayed in the city of Hamah for three days. Then they moved forward and did not stop traveling until they reached another city. They stayed there for three days as well, and from there they traveled until they entered the province of Diyar Bakr. > Sweetheart! How long must I wait, tested by such long suffering?
> No messenger comes to tell me where you stay.
> Ah me! Truly our time together was short enough;
> Would that Heaven would make this current separation even shorter!
> Now take my hand and open my robe, and you will see within
> How wasted my limbs are, yet I hide my frailty.

1 *Kaylúlah* is the "forty-winks" taken around noon. It is a *Sunnat* <note>original: "Sunnat"; a tradition or practice of the Prophet</note> of the Prophet, who said, "Take the midday siesta, for truly at this hour the devils do not sleep." *Aylúlah* is slumbering after morning prayers (our "beauty sleep"), which causes heaviness and laziness. *Ghaylúlah* is dozing around 9:00 a.m., which leads to poverty and misery. *Kaylúlah* (with the guttural "K" sound) is sleeping before evening prayers, and *Faylúlah* is slumbering after sunset—both are considered highly harmful. Zau al-Makan regained consciousness and saw that the moon had reached its zenith in the heavens. The breath of the morning breeze <gloss>1</gloss> blew upon him, and his heart was moved to longing and sadness. He cleared his throat and was about to recite some verses when the fireman asked him, "What are you doing?" 

Zau al-Makan answered, "I intend to recite some poetry so that I may quench the fire in my heart with it." 

The other replied, "You do not know what happened to me while you were unconscious, or how I escaped death only by tricking the Eunuch." 

"Tell me what happened," said Zau al-Makan. 

The stoker replied, "While you were in a faint, a Eunuch came up to me just now, carrying a long staff made of almond wood. He began looking into the faces of all the people as they lay asleep and asked me who it was that had recited the verses, since he found no one awake but me. I told him in reply that it was some passerby, a traveler; so he went away, and Allah delivered me from him. Otherwise, he would have killed me. But first, he said to me: 'If you hear him again, bring him to us.'" 

When Zau al-Makan heard this, he wept and said, "Who is it that would forbid me to recite? I will surely recite, no matter what happens to me; for I am near my own land and I fear no one." 

The fireman rejoined, "Your plan is nothing but a way to lose your life." 

Zau al-Makan retorted, "I must recite these verses." 

"Truly," said the stoker, "there must be a parting between you and me in this place, even though I had intended not to leave you until I had brought you to your native city and reunited you with your mother and father. You have stayed with me now for a year and a half, and I have never harmed you in any way. What is wrong with you, then, that you insist on reciting poetry, seeing that we are exhausted from walking and watching, and all the people are asleep because they need rest from their fatigue?" 

But Zau al-Makan answered, "I will not be turned away from my purpose." <gloss>2</gloss> Then grief overcame him; he stopped hiding his feelings and began repeating these couplets:

> Stand by the homes and greet the lords of the ruined dwellings;
> Cry out for an answer; perhaps a reply will be sent to you.
> If the night and absence trouble your soul, kindle a torch 
> Of longing, and light the darkness with a glowing ember <term>gleed</term>.

The stoker said, "Didn't you just see me sitting right where I am now? Don't you know my post? You know that no one can leave his place without the watchmen catching him. Then he kissed the eunuch's head and spoke kindly to him until he left. As soon as the eunuch was gone, the stoker woke Zau al-Makan and said to him, "Come, sit up, so I can tell you what happened."

So Zau al-Makan sat up, and his companion told him what had occurred. He answered, "Leave me alone; I won't pay any attention to this and I'm not afraid of anyone, for I am near my own country." <note>This reflects a popular Eastern saying: "A lion at home and a lamb abroad."</note>

The stoker said, "Why will you give in to your impulses and the devil? If you aren't afraid for yourself, I am afraid for you and for my own life, so for God's sake! Do not recite any more verses until you reach your own land. Indeed, I didn't think you were so stubborn. Don't you know that this lady is the wife of the Chamberlain and intends to punish you for disturbing her? Perhaps she is ill or restless from the fatigue of the journey and the distance from her home, and this is the second time she has sent the eunuch to look for you."

However, Zau al-Makan paid no attention to the fireman's words, but cried out a third time and began reciting these couplets:

> I flee from the critic’s harassment, <margin>*</margin> whose nagging distresses me greatly;
> He scolds and mocks me, not knowing <margin>*</margin> that he only makes my pain burn worse.
> The critic shouts, "He is comforted!" <margin>*</margin> while I say, "If only I could see my own dear land." <note>Arabic: *Hubb al-Watan* (patriotism or love of one's homeland). A religious tradition states that this "is part of faith" (*Min al-Iman*).</note>

### Now when it was the Seventy-fourth Night,

She said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the eunuch said to Zau al-Makan, "My lord, I have looked for you several times tonight, for my mistress summons you to her." Zau al-Makan asked, "And who is this bitch seeking me? May Allah curse her and her husband as well!" <note>He is meant to speak like a prince; he yields to a request but rejects a command.</note> And he began to insult the eunuch, who could not answer back because his mistress had ordered him not to harm Zau al-Makan, and only to bring him if he came of his own free will; if he refused to come, the eunuch was to give him the thousand gold coins.

So the eunuch began to speak kindly to him, saying, "My lord, take this purse and come with me. We will do you no injustice, my son, nor wrong you in any way. Our only goal is for you to walk with me to my mistress to receive her answer and return in health and safety. You shall also receive a generous gift as one who brings good news." When Zau al-Makan heard this, he stood up and went with the eunuch, walking among the sleeping people and stepping over them. When she heard this, her heart fluttered and she cried, “Let him recite some verses so that I may hear him from nearby, and afterward ask him his name, his status, and his homeland.” Then the eunuch went out to Zau al-Makan and said to him, “Recite what verses you know, for my lady is close by listening to you; afterward, I will ask you your name, your native country, and your circumstances.” 

He replied, “With love and gladness; but if you ask my name, it is erased, my history is lost, and my body is wasted away. I have a story whose beginning is unknown and whose end cannot be seen; and behold, I am just like one who has over-indulged in wine and has not spared himself—one who is afflicted with illnesses <term>distempers</term> and who wanders from his right mind, perplexed about his situation and drowned in a sea of thought.” 

When Nuzhat al-Zaman heard this, she broke into excessive weeping and sobbing and said to the eunuch, “Ask him if he has been separated from someone he loves, such as his mother or father.” The eunuch asked as she commanded him, and Zau al-Makan replied, “Yes, I have been parted from everyone I loved; but the dearest of all to me was my sister, from whom Fate has separated me.” 

When Nuzhat al-Zaman heard this, she exclaimed, “May Allah Almighty reunite him with the one he loves!”——And Shahrazad saw the dawn of day and stopped saying her permitted speech.

When Zau al-Makan heard this, he pressed his sister to his chest; tears streamed from his eyes from overwhelming joy, and he recited these verses <note>1</note>:—

> I long lamented that we fell apart, while repentant tears flowed from these eyes;
> And I swore, if Time unites us two once more, the word "separation" shall never be spoken by me again:
> Joy has so overwhelmed me that an excess of pleasure draws floods of tears from my eyes:
> Tears, O my eyes, have now become your habit; you weep for pleasure as you once wept for grief!

They sat for a while at the door of the litter until she said to him, "Come inside with me and tell me everything that has happened to you, and I will tell you what happened to me." So they went inside, and Zau al-Makan said, "You begin your story." Accordingly, she told him everything that had happened to her since their separation at the inn and what had occurred with the Bedouin; how the merchant had bought her from him, taken her to her brother Sharrkan, and sold her to him; how Sharrkan had freed her at the time of purchase; how he had made a marriage contract with her and consummated the marriage; and how the King, their father, had sent for her and requested her from Sharrkan. Then she said, "Praise be to God who has granted you to me and ordained that, just as we left our father together, so we shall return to him together!" And she added, "Truly, my brother Sharrkan gave me in marriage to this Chamberlain so that he might bring me back to my father. This is everything that has happened to me from beginning to end; so now, tell me how you have fared since I left you." Thereupon, he told her everything that had happened to him from start to finish; how God had seen fit to send the Stoker to him, and how he had traveled with him, and how the man had spent his own money on him and served him night and day. She praised the Stoker for this, and Zau al-Makan added, "In truth, my sister, this Stoker has dealt with me so kindly that even a lover would not do for his beloved, nor a father for his son. He fasted so that I could eat, and he walked while he made me ride; I owe my life to him." She replied, "God willing, we will reward him for all this to the best of our ability." Then she called—

When the Chamberlain heard the story, he knew it to be the truth; its clear reality became apparent to him, and he was certain that he had become King Omar bin al-Nu'uman's son-in-law. So he said to himself, "It will be my fate to be appointed viceroy of some province.<gloss>A reference to the 'island' promised to the character Sancho Panza in Cervantes' *Don Quixote*.</gloss>"

Thereupon, Nuzhat al-Zaman said, "We are now near our own country, and I wish to be left alone with my brother so that we may enjoy each other's company and have our fill of it before we reach Baghdad; for we have been parted for a long, long time." 

"Let it be as you command," replied the Chamberlain. Going out from them, he sent them wax candles and various kinds of sweets, along with three of the costliest suits of clothes for Zau al-Makan. Then he returned to the litter and told her of the good things he had done. Nuzhat al-Zaman said to him, "Tell the Eunuch to bring me the Fireman and give him a horse to ride. Provide him with a tray of food every morning and evening, and forbid him from leaving us." 

The Chamberlain called the <term>Castrato</term> and ordered him to do as she requested. He replied, "I hear and I obey." Taking his pages with him, he went out in search of the <term>Stoker</term> <note>The Fireman who helped Zau al-Makan.</note> until he found him at the rear of the caravan, cinching the saddle on his donkey and preparing to flee. Tears were running down his cheeks out of fear for his life and grief over his separation from Zau al-Makan. He was saying to himself, "Indeed, I warned him for the love of Allah, but he would not listen to me. Oh, if only I knew what has become of him!" Before he had finished speaking, the Eunuch was standing over him while the pages surrounded him.

### Now when it was the Seventy-sixth Night,

She said, It has reached me, O auspicious King, that when the Stoker girthed his donkey for flight and spoke to himself, saying, “Oh, if only I knew what has become of him!”; before he had finished speaking, the <term>Castrato</term> <note>A eunuch servant.</note> was standing by his head. The Stoker’s side-muscles quivered for fear and he lifted up his voice and cried, “Truly he does not know the value of the good favors I have done him! I believe he has denounced me to the Eunuch (which is why these pages surround me) and he has made me an accomplice in his crime.” 

Then the effeminate one shouted at him, saying, “Who was it that recited the verses? O liar! Why did you say: ‘I never repeated these couplets, nor do I know who repeated them,’ when it was your companion? But now I will not leave you between this place and Baghdad, and what happens to your comrade shall happen to you.” 

The Fireman said, “What I feared has befallen me.” And he repeated this couplet:

> It was as I feared, foreseeing the coming troubles;
> But to Allah we are all returning. <note>original: "’Twas as I feared the coming ills discerning: ◦ But unto Allah we are all returning."</note>

But when the Stoker saw himself beset by the pages, he despaired for his life and, turning to the Eunuch, said to him, “O Chief, I am neither this youth’s brother nor am I kin to him, nor is he <term>sib</term> <note>Related or akin.</note> to me; but I was a Fireman in a <term>Hammam</term> <note>A public bathhouse.</note> and found him cast out, in his sickness, on the dung-heap.”
