# Alf Laylah wa Laylah.

They ate from one dish. <note>Eating from the same dish was a traditional gesture of peace and safety, assuring the guest that they were not in danger.</note> Then the Eunuch ordered his servants to bring a <term>gugglet</term> <note>A long-necked earthen water bottle used to keep liquids cool.</note> of sugared sherbet and, after drinking some himself, gave it to the Stoker, who drank. Yet all the while, the Stoker's tears never dried because of his fear for his life and his grief over being separated from Zau al-Makan, as well as the hardships they had faced together in their travels. 

So they both traveled on with the caravan. The Chamberlain alternately rode by the door of his wife’s litter to attend to Zau al-Makan and his sister, and kept an eye on the Stoker. Meanwhile, Nuzhat al-Zaman and her brother occupied themselves with conversation and mutual comfort. They continued in this manner until they were within three days’ journey of Baghdad. 

Here they stopped at evening and rested until morning broke. As they woke and were about to load the animals, they suddenly saw a great cloud of dust far off that darkened the sky until it became as black as the gloomiest night. <note>This marks the end of the focus on the brother and sister's personal journey, and the epic romance returns to the larger military and political conflicts of the story.</note> 

Upon seeing this, the Chamberlain cried out to them, “Stop, and delay your loading!” Then, mounting his horse with his <term>Mamelukes</term> <note>An elite class of horse-mounted warrior-slaves.</note>, he rode forward toward the dust cloud. When they drew near, a numerous, conquering army suddenly appeared beneath the dust like the rising tide of the sea, complete with flags, standards, drums, kettledrums, horsemen, and footmen. 

The Chamberlain was amazed by this. When the troops saw him, a group of five hundred cavalrymen detached themselves from the main body, fell upon him and his entourage, and surrounded them—five soldiers for every one of his. 

The Chamberlain said to them, “What is the matter? What are these troops, and why are you doing this to us?” 

They asked, “Who are you? Where do you come from, and where are you going?” 

He answered, “I am the Chamberlain of the Emir of Damascus, King Sharrkan, son of Omar bin al-Nu’uman, Lord of Baghdad and of the land of Khorasan. I am bringing tribute and presents from him to his father in Baghdad.” 

When the horsemen heard his words, they let their head-kerchiefs fall over their faces and wept, saying, “In truth, King Omar is dead; he did not die naturally, but was poisoned. Go forward; no harm shall come to you until you reach his Grand Vizier, Dandan.”

# Tale of King Omar bin al-Nu’uman and his Sons.

He caught up with the army and sought an audience with the Wazir <note>Also spelled Vizier; a high-ranking political advisor or minister.</note> Dandan. The Wazir granted the interview and ordered a halt to the march. He had his pavilion pitched, sat down on a couch inside, and commanded that the Chamberlain be admitted. He then invited him to be seated and questioned him. The Chamberlain replied that he was the Chamberlain to the Emir of Damascus and was traveling to King Omar with gifts and the tribute of Syria. 

When the Wazir heard King Omar’s name mentioned, he wept and said, “King Omar has died from poison. Upon his death, the people fell into disputes over who should succeed him, until they were on the verge of killing one another. However, the notables, the grandees, and the four <term>Kazis</term> <note>Islamic judges or magistrates.</note> intervened. Everyone agreed to refer the matter to the decision of the four judges and that no one should oppose them. So it was agreed that we should go to Damascus and fetch the King’s son, Sharrkan, to make him Sultan over his father’s realm. Among them were some who would have chosen the younger son, Zau al-Makan; for, they said, his name means ‘Light of the Place,’ and he has a sister named Nuzhat al-Zaman, meaning ‘Delight of the Time.’ But they set out five years ago for the <term>Hijaz</term> <note>The western region of the Arabian Peninsula, containing Mecca and Medina.</note>, and no one knows what has become of them.” 

When the Chamberlain heard this, he knew that his wife had told him the truth about her adventures. He felt deep grief over the death of King Omar, although he also rejoiced greatly, especially at the arrival of Zau al-Makan, knowing that he would now become the Sultan of Baghdad in his father’s place.

The Chamberlain then went in to her and spoke with her and her brother. They both wept for their father and asked how he had been killed, but the Chamberlain answered, “The Wazir <note>A high-ranking political advisor or minister.</note> Dandan has all the news; he will arrive tomorrow leading the entire army. It only remains for you, O King, to do as they advise, since they have unanimously chosen you as Sultan. If you do not accept, they will choose someone else, and your life would not be safe under another Sultan. He might kill you, or discord might break out between the two of you, and the kingdom would be lost to both.” 

Zau al-Makan bowed his head for a moment and then said, “I accept this position,” for there was truly no way to refuse. He was certain that the Chamberlain had given him wise and honest counsel and set him on the right path. Then he added, “O my uncle, what shall I do about my brother Sharrkan?” 

“O my son,” the Chamberlain replied, “your brother will be Sultan of Damascus, and you will be Sultan of Baghdad. So take heart and prepare yourself.” 

Zau al-Makan accepted this, and the Chamberlain presented him with a suit of royal clothing and a state dagger<gloss>1</gloss> that the Wazir Dandan had brought with him. After leaving him, the Chamberlain ordered the tent-pitchers to find a high spot of ground and set up a large pavilion where the Sultan could sit to receive the Emirs <note>Commanders or princes.</note> and Grandees <note>High-ranking noblemen.</note>. ### Now when it was the Seventy-eighth Night,

She said: I have heard, O fortunate King, that when the Chamberlain ordered the tent-pitchers to set up a pavilion large enough to receive the subjects flocking to their Sultan, they erected a magnificent Shahmiyanah¹ fit for kings. As they finished their work, a cloud of dust rose high in the air; the breeze lifted it, revealing a conquering army beneath. It soon became clear that this was the army of Baghdad and Khorasan, led by the Wazir Dandan. Everyone in the army rejoiced at the accession <note>The formal act of taking a high office, such as a throne.</note> of the "Light of the Place" <note>The literal translation of the name Zau al-Makan.</note>. 

Now Zau al-Makan had put on royal robes and strapped on the sword of state. The Chamberlain brought him a horse and he mounted it, surrounded by the Mamelukes <note>A class of soldier-slaves who reached high political and military standing.</note> and the entire company from the tents who followed on foot to serve him. He rode until he reached the great pavilion. There he sat down and laid the royal dagger across his thighs, while the Chamberlain stood in attendance. His armed slaves stationed themselves under the entrance awning of the Shahmiyanah with drawn swords in their hands. 

Soon the troops and the army arrived and requested entrance. The Chamberlain went to Zau al-Makan and asked his permission, and the King ordered them to be admitted ten at a time. The Chamberlain informed them of the King’s commands, to which they replied, "We hear and we obey." They all lined up before the pavilion entrance. Then the Chamberlain took ten of them and led them through the vestibule into the presence of Sultan Zau al-Makan. When they saw him, they were struck with awe, but he received them with great kindness and promised them every favor. They congratulated him on his safe return and called for God's blessings upon him. Afterward, they took an oath of loyalty, swearing never to oppose him in anything; they kissed the ground before him and withdrew. Then another ten entered, and he treated them just as he had treated the first group. They continued to enter, ten by ten, until no one was left.

### Now when it was the Seventy-ninth Night,

She said: It has reached me, O auspicious King, that the Vizier Dandan said to King Zau al-Makan: Your father, who is now of blessed memory, glanced at the young women and was pleased by them. He said to them, “Let each and every one of you let me hear something of what she knows regarding the history of ancient people and of those who lived long ago!” Thereupon, one of them came forward and, kissing the ground before him, spoke as follows <note>Burton's original note suggests that the following academic speeches were intended for serious students of the text.</note>:

“Know, O King, that it is proper for a well-bred person to avoid impertinence and to adorn themselves with excellence, to observe Divine commands, and to avoid mortal sins. To this, one should apply themselves with the diligence of someone who knows that if they stray from that path, they will fall into ruin; for the foundation of good breeding is virtuous behavior. And know that the chief cause and reason for man’s existence is the pursuit of eternal life, and the right way to achieve that is through the service of God <note>original: "Allah"</note>. Therefore, it is necessary for you to deal kindly with the people, and do not stray from this rule."

For the higher men are in status, the more they need prudence and foresight; indeed, monarchs need this more than most people, for the general public throw themselves into matters without thinking about the outcome. Be generous with your life and your wealth in the way of God <note>original: "Allah"</note>, and know that if an enemy argues with you, you may dispute with him and defeat him with proofs and be protected against him. 

But as for your friend, there is no one who can judge between you and him except righteousness and fair dealing. Therefore, choose your friend for yourself after you have tested him. If he is of the "brotherhood of the afterlife," <margin>That is, those who look for "another and a better" world.</margin> let him be diligent in observing the external rules of the Holy Law and skilled in its inner meaning as much as possible. And if he is of the "brotherhood of the world," let him be free-born and sincere, being neither a fool nor a perverse person; for a fool is the kind of man that even his parents might well flee from, and a liar cannot be a true friend. 

Indeed, the word "Friend" <note>original: "Siddík"</note> <margin>The title of Caliph Abu Bakr because he bore truthful witness to the Apostle's mission or, as others say, he confirmed the "Ascension" <note>original: "Mi'ráj"</note> or nocturnal journey to Heaven.</margin> is derived from "Truth" <note>original: "Sidk"</note> that wells up from the bottom of the heart; and how can this be the case when falsehood is obvious on the tongue? Know also that following the Law benefits the person who practices it; so love your brother if he has this quality and do not cast him off, even if you see something in him that bothers <term>irketh</term> you. For a friend is not like a wife, whom one can divorce and remarry; rather, his heart is like glass: once broken, it cannot be mended. And God bless the one who said:

->Beware how you hurt a person with a wounded heart; ◦ It is hard to win back a heart you have offended:<-
->For indeed, when love is driven from the heart, ◦ Like broken glass, it can never be mended.<-

God <note>original: "Allah"</note> afflicts him with something greater; he who follows his own whims neglects his duties, and he who listens to a slanderer loses a true friend. If someone thinks well of you, fulfill their good opinion of you. He who goes too far in an argument sins, and he who does not stand guard against injustice is not safe from the sword. 

Now I will tell you something of the duties of judges <note>original: "Kazis"</note> and magistrates. Know, O King, that no judgment serves the cause of justice unless it is given after positive proof. It is the duty of the judge to treat all people as equals, so that the powerful do not crave to oppress others and the lowly do not despair of receiving justice. Furthermore, he should require proof from the accuser and require an oath from the defendant. Mediation is allowed between Muslims, unless it is a compromise that permits what is forbidden or forbids what is permitted.<sup>1</sup> 

If you have done anything during the day where your reasoning was doubtful but your good intention is proven, you (O Judge) should return to what is right; for doing justice is a religious obligation, and returning to what is right is better than persisting in what is wrong. Then, O Judge, you should study precedents and the law relevant to the case and provide equal justice to the litigants, while keeping your eyes fixed on the truth and committing your affairs to God—may He be praised and exalted! 

Require proof from the accuser, and if he provides evidence, let him receive the benefit of it; if not, require the defendant to take an oath, for this is the decree of God. Accept the testimony of competent Muslim witnesses against one another, for Almighty God has commanded judges to judge by outward appearances, while He Himself takes charge of inner and secret matters. A judge should also avoid giving a judgment while suffering from the stress of pain or hunger,<sup>2</sup> and in his decisions between people, he should seek the favor of Almighty God. For if a person's intent is pure and he is at peace with himself, God will protect him in his dealings with others. 

Al-Zuhri<sup>3</sup> said, "There are three things for which, if they are found in a judge, he should be removed from office: if he honors the wicked, if he loves praise, and if he fears being dismissed." 

And Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz once dismissed a judge, who asked him, "Why have you dismissed me?"

### Now when it was the Eighty-first Night,

She continued: It has reached me, O auspicious King, that the Vizier <note>original: "Wazir"</note> Dandan said to Zau al-Makan:—Thus spoke the second handmaid to the King who has found mercy, Omar bin al-Nu'uman. And Ghaus bin Abdillah said: There were two brothers among the children of Israel, one of whom said to the other, 'What is the most <term>perilous</term> <note>meaning: spiritually dangerous</note> thing you have ever done?' He rejoined, 'When I stand up to pray, I am afraid that I am doing it only for the sake of the reward.' Among the sayings of Sufyan al-Thawri, with which he advised Ali bin al-Hasan al-Salami, was: "Be a man of truth and beware of lies, treachery, hypocrisy, and pride. Do not be indebted to anyone except Him who is merciful to His debtors; and let your companion be one who shall detach you from the world. Be ever mindful of death and be constant in seeking forgiveness from Allah, and in beseeching Allah for peace for what remains of your life. Counsel every True Believer when he asks you concerning the things of his faith; and beware of betraying a Believer, for whoever betrays a Believer, betrays Allah and His Messenger. Avoid disputes and litigation; and leave that which causes doubt in you for things which breed no doubt:<note>2</note> so shall you be at peace. Command what is good and forbid what is evil: so shall you be loved by Allah. Adorn your inner self and Allah shall adorn your outer self. Accept the apology of him who excuses himself to you, and do not hate any of the Muslims. Draw near to those who withdraw from you and forgive those who mistreat you: so shall you be the friend of the Prophets. Let your affairs, both public and private, be in Allah's charge, and fear Him with the fear of one who knows he is dead and who journeys toward the Resurrection and the Place of Judgment before the hands of the Lord of Awe; and remember that you are destined for one of two houses: either for eternal Heaven or for the burning fires of Hell."

Thereupon the old woman sat down beside the young women. Now when your father, who has found mercy <note>A traditional way of referring to the deceased</note>, heard their discourse, he knew that they were the most accomplished people of their time; and, seeing their beauty and—

# Tale of King Omar bin al-Nu'uman and his Sons.

Because of their beauty and the depth of their wisdom and knowledge, he showed them great favor. Moreover, he turned his attention to the elderly lady and treated her with honor. He set aside the palace that had once housed Princess Abrizah, daughter of the King of Greece, for her and her damsels, and he ordered that all the luxuries they needed be brought there. They stayed with him for ten days, and the old woman remained with them. Whenever the King visited them, he found her absorbed in prayer, keeping watch by night and fasting by day. Because of this, love for her took hold of his heart, and he said to me, "O Wazir, truly this old woman is one of the godly, and I feel a great sense of awe for her."

On the eleventh day, the King visited her so that he might pay her the price for the maidens; but she said to him, "O King, know that the price of these maidens is beyond the means of men. Indeed, I do not seek gold, silver, or jewels for them, whether in small or large amounts." When your father heard these words, he wondered and asked her, "O my lady, what then is their price?" She answered, "I will not sell them to you except on the condition that you fast—keeping watch by night for a whole month and abstaining from food by day—all for the love of Allah Almighty. If you do this, they are your property to use in your palace as you please."

The King marveled at the perfection of her righteousness, piety, and self-denial. She rose in his estimation, and he said, "May Allah allow this pious woman to benefit us!" Then he agreed to fast for a month as she had stipulated, and she said to him, "I will help you with the prayers I offer for you; now, bring me a water jug." <term>gugglet: a long-necked water jug, often made of porous clay to keep water cool</term> They brought one, and she took it, recited over it, and whispered incantations. She sat for an hour speaking in a language that no one understood or recognized. Finally, she covered it with a cloth and, sealing it with her signet ring, gave it to your father, saying, "When you have fasted the first ten days, break your fast on the eleventh night with what is in this jug. It will remove worldly desires from your heart and fill it with light and faith. As for me, tomorrow I will go out to my brothers, the Invisible Guardians,<note>original: "Rijál al-Ghayb"—literally 'Men of the Unseen.' This refers to a hierarchy of saints or spirits in Islamic mysticism who are believed to remain hidden from the physical world but influence human affairs.</note> for I long for them; but I will return to you."

<note>The Arabic term *Rijál al-Ghayb* refers to a concept somewhat like the "Himalayan Brothers" of modern occultism. In the *Qanoon-e-Islam* by Herklots, there is a detailed description of these "Men of the Unseen" (*Mardán-i-Ghayb* in Persian). They are described as a class of people who travel on clouds, remaining invisible while moving in a circular orbit around the world, similar to the Hindu *Lokapálas* (world guardians). To ensure a journey ends well, a traveler must ensure these beings are behind them or to their left, rather than in front or to their right. Tables and mnemonic verses are often used to determine their current position.</note>

## Now when it was the Eighty-seventh Night,

She said: I have heard, O fortunate King, that Zau al-Makan ordered the Chamberlain to bring before him what he had brought of the tribute from Damascus; and, when he was shown the chests of money, rarities, and jewels, he took them and distributed them all among the troops until nothing was left. # Now when the Eighty-eighth Night arrived,

She said, "I have heard, O fortunate King, that Sharrkan asked his brother Zau al-Makan, 'Have you rewarded the <term>Fireman</term> <note>The man who stoked the fires at the bath-house and assisted Zau al-Makan during his poverty.</note> for his kindness?' and he answered, 'O my brother, I have not rewarded him yet, but God willing <note>original: "Inshallah"</note>, I will compensate him when I return from this raid and find the time to do so.' She told them to place her in a chest and said, “Cry out the Declaration of Unity² <note>original: "Refrain of Unity"</note> and do not fear any harm from it!” They replied, “How can we beat you, when you are our sovereign lady, Zat al-Dawahi, the mother of the King we take pride in?” Then she said, “We do not blame or criticize someone who goes to the toilet <term>original: "jakes"</term>; in times of necessity, an evil act becomes a good deed. When you have placed me in the chest, take it and treat it as one of your bales of goods. Place it on the back of a mule and travel with it and the other merchandise through the Muslim camp, and do not fear any blame. If any of the Muslims stop you, give up the mules and their cargo and go to their King, Zau al-Makan, to beg for his protection, saying: ‘We were in the land of the Christians <term>original: "Infidels"</term> and they took nothing from us, but instead gave us a passport so that no one would hinder us or cause us misfortune.’ If he asks you, ‘What profit did you make from your property in the land of the Romans <term>original: "Roum"</term>?’ answer him: ‘Our profit was the rescue of a pious man who had been kept in an underground cell for nearly fifteen years, crying out for help while no one helped him. Instead, the Christians tortured him day and night. We did not know about this; however, after we had stayed in Constantinople for some time, sold our goods, and bought others in their place, we prepared to return to our native land. We spent that night talking about our journey, and when day broke, we saw a human form pictured upon the wall. As we approached it, it moved and said: “O Muslims, is there anyone among you who wishes to gain the favor of the Lord of the Three Worlds?³” “How so?” we asked; and the figure answered: “Know that Allah has made me speak to you, to the—’”

---

^1 Quran, 2:149. Hence the common idea that Martyrs are still alive in the flesh. See my *Pilgrimage* (ii. 110 and elsewhere) for the romantic and picturesque consequences of that belief. The Commentators (Jalal al-Din, etc.) play tricks with the Quranic words, "they (martyrs) are not dead but living" (3:179) by placing the happy souls in the crops of green birds which eat of the fruits and drink of the waters of Paradise; whereas the outcasts and the very wicked are deposited in black birds which drain the pus <note>original: "sanies"</note> and the boiling waters of Hell. Among the Greeks, a body remaining intact long after death suggests a formal curse <note>original: "Anathema Maranatha"</note>; it is the opposite for Catholic Christians (Boccaccio iv. 5, the "Pot of Basil"). Concerning this belief, see Maundrell’s Letter of 1698.

^2 Sinai <note>original: "Tor"</note> is "Mount Sinai" in the Quran (95:1). I have only to repeat my opinion concerning the present site so called: "It is evident that Mount Serbal dates only from the early days of Coptic Christianity; that Mount Moses <note>original: "Jebel Musa"</note>, its Greek rival, rose after the visions of Helena in the fourth century; while the building of the Convent by Justinian belongs to 527 A.D. Ras Safsafah, its rival to the north, is a very recent matter, and may be called the invention of Robinson; and Mount Catherine <note>original: "Jebel Katerina"</note>, to the south, is the property of Rüppell" (*Midian Revisited* i., 237.). I would therefore call the "Sinaitic" Peninsula the Peninsula of Paran in ancient times and the Peninsula of Sinai <note>original: "Tor"</note> (from its chief port) in our own time. It is still my conviction that the true Mount Sinai will be found in Mount Araif <note>original: "Jabal Aráif"</note>, or some such unimportant height to the north of the modern Hajj road from Suez to Akabah. Even about the name (which the Quran writes "Saina" and "Sinin") there is a dispute: It is usually derived from the root "Sanah," meaning a thorn-bush <note>original: "sentis"</note>; but this is not satisfactory. Our eminent Assyriologist, Professor Sayce, would connect it with "Sin," the Assyrian Moon-god, just as Mount Nebo is connected with the Sun-god; and he expects to find there the ruins of a lunar temple <note>original: "fane"</note> just as a solar temple stands on Baal-Zephon <note>original: "Ba'al Zapuna"</note> or the classical Mount Casius.

^3 Alluding to the miracle of Aaron's rod (the gift of Jethro) as related in the Quran (chapters 7, 20, etc.), where the Egyptian sorcerers threw down thick ropes which, by their magic, twisted and coiled like serpents.

^4 Arabic "Ayat," literally "signs," here meaning "miracles of the truth" (as above). Quranic verses <note>original: "versets"</note> as opposed to chapters. The ranks of the enemy represent the latter, while sword-cuts represent the former—a very persuasive mode of preaching.

When the old woman finished her poem, her eyes overflowed with tears and her forehead shone like a bright light under the ointment she wore. Sharrkan stood up, kissed her hand, and ordered food to be brought to her. However, she refused it, saying, “I have not broken my fast during the day for fifteen years. How could I break it now, when my Lord has been so generous to me by delivering me from the captivity of the non-believers and removing a burden from me that was more painful than the fires of hell? So, when night fell, Sharrkan and Zau al-Makan came and served her food, saying, “Eat, O holy one!” But she replied, “This is no time for eating; it is the time for worshipping the King of Recompense.” Then she stood in the prayer niche and continued praying until the night was over. She did not stop behaving in this manner for three days and nights, only sitting down during the *Salam*, or the salutation<gloss>1</gloss> that ends the various prayers. 

When Zau al-Makan saw her behaving in this way, a firm belief in her took hold of his heart. He said to Sharrkan, “Have a tent of scented leather set up for this holy man, and assign a personal servant to wait on him.” On the fourth day, she called for food, so they brought her all kinds of meats that could tempt the senses or delight the eyes; however, she would eat only a piece of flatbread with salt. Sharrkan said to Zau al-Makan, “Truly, this man carries his rejection of the world to the furthest extreme. If it were not for this Holy War, I would join him and worship God <note>original: "Allah"</note> in his service until I died. Now, I want to enter his tent and talk with him for a while.”

### Now when it was the Ninety-eighth Night,

She said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that when the non-believers had seized King Zau al-Makan and the Minister <term>Wazir</term> Dandan, they said to the two of them, "Is there anyone else with you two, so that we may seize him as well?"

They began to lament, saying to each other, "Truly, opposing holy men leads to greater distress than this, and we are being punished by the hardship that has befallen us."

This is what happened to Zau al-Makan and the Minister <term>Wazir</term> Dandan; but as for King Sharrkan, he passed that night in the cavern with his comrades. When dawn broke and he had performed the morning prayer, he and his men made ready to do battle with the non-believers. He encouraged them and promised them every success.

Then they marched out until they were close to the non-believers. When the enemy saw them from afar, they cried out to them, saying, "O Muslims <term>Moslems</term>, we have captured your Sultan and your Minister <term>Wazir</term> who directs your affairs. Unless you stop fighting us, we will kill every last one of you! But if you surrender, we will take you to our King, who will make peace with you on the condition that you leave our country and return home and do not harm us in any way, and we will do you no harm in return. If you accept, it will be well for you; but if you refuse, nothing remains for you but death. We have told you the truth, and this is our last word to you."

When Sharrkan heard this and was certain of the capture of his brother and the Minister <term>Wazir</term> Dandan, he was overwhelmed with grief and wept. His strength failed him, and, certain of death, he said to himself, "I wish I knew the reason for their capture! Did they fail to respect the holy man or disobey him, or what was the matter?"

Then they sprang up to battle the non-believers and killed great numbers of them. That day, the brave were distinguished from the cowards, and sword and spear were stained with blood; for the non-believers flocked toward them like flies to a drink, from both hill and plain. But Sharrkan and his men did not cease to wage the fight of...

Those who did not fear to die, nor let death stop them from the pursuit of victory, fought until the valley flowed with blood and the earth was covered with the fallen. When night fell, the armies separated, each returning to its own camp. The Muslims returned to the cavern where the extent of their losses was clear to them: few of them remained, and they had no hope except for Allah and the scimitar <term>a curved oriental sword</term>. That day, thirty-five of the leading commanders <term>Emirs</term> had been killed, though they had killed thousands of the non-believers, both infantry and cavalry. When Sharrkan saw this, it distressed him and he asked his comrades, “What shall we do?” To which all answered, “Whatever Almighty Allah wills shall happen to us.” 

On the morning of the second day, Sharrkan said to the remnant of his troop, “If you go out to fight, not one of you will survive, and we have very little food and water left. Therefore, I think it would be better for you to draw your swords and stand at the mouth of this cavern to prevent anyone from entering. Perhaps the holy man has reached the Muslim army and may return with ten thousand horsemen to help us in our fight against the non-believers; for it is likely the unfaithful failed to notice him and those with him.” They replied, “This is the better course to take, and we have no doubt of its wisdom.” 

So the troop went out and guarded the mouth of the cavern, standing by its walls; they killed every one of the non-believers who tried to enter. In this way, they warded off the enemy from the opening of the cave and patiently endured all such attacks until the day ended and the night came on dark and gloomy.

And Shahrazad noticed the dawn of day and stopped her permitted speech.

Then the non-believers said to one another, “When will these days of battle end? We are weary of fighting the...”

Then, as soon as the night was pitch black, the non-believers busied themselves with feasting and celebration; they called for wine and drank until they all fell unconscious on their backs. Sharrkan and his brother, Zau al-Makan, were in confinement, as were his fellow knights. The elder brother turned to the younger and said to him, "O my brother, how shall we win our freedom?" 

"By Allah," replied Zau al-Makan, "I do not know, for here we are like birds in a cage." 

Then Sharrkan grew furious and sighed with intense rage; he stretched himself until his bonds burst <term>brast</term> asunder. Being free, he arose and went to the Captain of the guard. Taking the keys to the fetters from his pocket, he freed Zau al-Makan, the Vizier <term>Wazir</term> Dandan, and the rest of his men. Then he turned to the two of them and said, "I intend to kill three of these non-believers and put on their clothes—the three of us—so that we shall be disguised as Greeks. Zau al-Makan replied, "This plan is not good. We would do better to make our way to our own army and not say a word; for if we cry out 'God is Great!', they will wake up and attack us, and not one of us will escape." 

Sharrkan rejoined, "By God, even if they should wake, it does not matter. I long for you to follow my plan, for nothing but good can come of it!"

### Now when it was the full Hundredth Night,

She said: I have heard, O fortunate King, that Sharrkan spoke this way: "I desire that you agree to this plan of mine, for nothing but good can come of it." So they agreed to it and climbed to the mountain peak and shouted, "God is Great!" <note>original: "Allaho Akbar"</note>; and the hills, trees, and rocks echoed their "God is Great!" for fear of the Almighty. The Unbelievers heard it and cried out to one another, put on their armor, and said, "The enemy is upon us, by the truth of the Messiah!" Then they fell upon one another and killed more of their own men than anyone knows except Almighty God. As soon as it was dawn, they looked for the captives but found no trace of them. Their captains said, "The ones who did this were the prisoners in our possession; get up, then, and after them in all haste until you overtake them, when we will make them drink from the cup of retribution; and do not let fright or the panic of a sudden awakening possess you." So they took horse and rode after the fugitives, and in the blink of an eye they overtook and surrounded them. 

Now when Zau al-Makan saw this, he was seized with growing terror and said to his brother, "What I feared would happen has come upon us, and now it only remains for us to fight for the Faith." But Sharrkan preferred to remain silent. Then Zau al-Makan and his companions rushed down from the hilltop, shouting, "God is Great!" <note>original: "Allaho Akbar"</note> and his men repeated the war cry and prepared themselves to fight and to sacrifice their lives in the service of the Lord of the Faithful. While they were in this state, they suddenly heard many voices crying, "There is no god but God! God is most great! Peace and salvation be upon the Messenger, the Bringer of Good News and the Warner!" <note>i.e., Muhammad, who promised Heaven and threatened Hell.</note> So they turned toward the sound and saw a company of Muslims who believed in one God, charging toward them. At this, their hearts were encouraged, and Sharrkan charged at the Unbelievers, crying out, "There is no god but God! God is most great!" He and those with him fought so hard that the earth shook as if by an earthquake, and the army of Unbelievers broke apart and fled into the mountains. The Muslims followed them with spear-thrusts and sword-blows; and Zau al-Makan and his Muslim comrades did not stop striking the hosts of the Unbeliever enemy, severing heads from bodies until day—

The world darkened, and as night fell, their vision grew dim. At this, the Muslims gathered together and spent the night in mutual congratulations. When morning dawned and the daybreak shone with its light and splendor, they saw Bahram, the captain of the Daylamites, and Rustam, the captain of the Turks, advancing to join them with twenty thousand horsemen as fierce as lions. As soon as they saw Zau al-Makan, the riders dismounted and saluted him, kissing the ground in front of him. He said to them, "Rejoice in the glad tidings of the victory of the Muslims and the defeat of the tribe of unbelievers!" Then they congratulated one another on their deliverance and on the greatness of their reward after the Day of Resurrection.

Now, the reason the reinforcements arrived at that place was this: when the Emir Bahram, the Emir Rustam, and the Chief Chamberlain—leading the Muslim host with flags waving high—came in sight of Constantinople, they saw that the Christians <note>original: "Nazarenes"</note> had mounted the walls and manned the towers and forts. The defenders had put everything in order for a defense as soon as they learned of the approach of the army of Islam and the Mohammedan banners. They heard the clash of arms, the noise of war-cries, and the tramp of horses' hooves. From their lookouts, they beheld the Muslims with their standards and ensigns of the Faith of Unity <note>The Islamic doctrine of Tawhid</note> under the dust clouds; they looked like a flight of locusts or rain clouds pouring down rain. The voices of the Muslims chanting the Koran and glorifying the Compassionate One reached their ears. 

The infidels knew of the approach of this host through the schemes of Zat al-Dawahi, with her cunning and wickedness,¹ her slander and her contrivances. The armies of Islam drew near like a swelling sea because of the great number of footmen, horsemen, women, and children. Then the General of the Turks said to the General of the Daylamites, "O Emir, in truth, we are in jeopardy because of the great number of the enemy on the walls. Look at those bulwarks and at this sea of people like crashing waves. Indeed, those infidels outnumber us a hundredfold, and we cannot be safe from spies who may inform them that we are without a Sultan. Truly, we are in danger from these enemies, whose numbers are beyond counting and whose resources cannot be stopped, especially in the absence of King Zau al-Makan and—"

<note>Here "Kahwah" (coffee) is used in its original sense of strong old wine. When the Chamberlain and the Muslims heard these words, their spirits fell and they wept; but Zat al-Dawahi said to them, "Seek help from Allah and bear this tribulation patiently; for you have the example of the people of Muhammad who came before you. Allah has prepared Paradise and its palaces for those who die as martyrs; and everyone must eventually die, but it is most praiseworthy to die while fighting for the Faith."

Hearing this speech from the accursed old woman, the Chamberlain called for the Emir Bahram’s brother, a knight named Tarkásh. Choosing ten thousand horsemen for him—riders famous for their strength—he ordered him to set out at once. So he rode forth and marched all that day and the entire following night until he neared the Muslims.

## Now when it was the Hundred-and-second Night,

She said: It has reached me, O auspicious King, that when Sharrkan saw the Muslims in a defeated state, and the Chamberlain on the brink of retreat and flight, and the havoc of the sword being dealt among the righteous and the wrongdoers alike, the cause of this weakness among the Muslims was that the accursed old woman, Zat al-Dawahi, the enemy of the Faith, had been at work. After seeing that Bahram and Rustam had set forward with their troops to join Sharrkan and his brother Zau al-Makan, she went to the camp of the Muslims before Constantinople and arranged the mission of the Emir Tarkash, as has been mentioned before. So they lowered a string for her, and she tied a letter to it, the content of which was as follows:

As soon as morning dawned and day broke in brilliance and splendor, the Muslims marched out to the plain, and the non-believers <note>Kafirs</note> prepared to thrust and cut. He rode a stallion like Abjar, which was the famous charger of Antar, and its coat was as jet black as the poet describes:

> -> On the swift racer, outracing a glance, he speeds, <-
> -> As though he would seize Fate itself by the collar. <-
> -> His steed's black coat is of the darkest jet, <-

Then each warrior rushed upon his opponent, parrying blows and demonstrating the marvelous skills they possessed. They continued advancing and retreating until the hearts of the bystanders grew tense and they grew weary of waiting for the outcome. At last, Zau al-Makan shouted his war cry and rushed upon Hardub, King of Caesarea,<sup>2</sup> striking him with a blow that severed his head from his body and killed him on the spot. When the non-believers saw this, they charged as one united body upon Zau al-Makan, who met them in the middle of the field. They engaged in hacking and thrusting <term>foining</term> until blood ran in streams. Then the Muslims cried out, "God is Most Great!" <note>Allaho Akbar</note> and "There is no god but God!"; they also invoked blessings for the Prophet, the bringer of glad tidings and warnings. A great fight ensued, but Allah granted victory to the faithful and defeat to the faithless. The Vizier <note>Wazir</note> Dandan shouted, "Take your revenge for King Omar bin al-Nu'uman and his son Sharrkan!" He uncovered his head and called out to the Turks. At his side were more than twenty thousand cavalry, and they all charged with him as one man. The non-believers found no way to save their lives except by fleeing. They turned tail to run while the sharp swords caused great slaughter. The Muslims killed about fifty thousand of their cavalry that day and captured more than that number; many people were also killed while trying to escape.

<sup>1</sup> Racing was and remains a favorite pastime with those horse-lovers <term>hippomanists</term>, the Arabs; however, it contrasts strongly with our modern version, as it is a trial of endurance rather than just speed. The Prophet is said to have limited betting with these words: "There shall be no wagering except on the camel's foot, the hoof of a horse or donkey, or the arrow-head or lance-head."
<sup>2</sup> In the Macan Edition, this is "**Armenia**," which has appeared before. The author or scribe here understands "**Caesarea**" not as the old Strato's Tower <note>original: "Turris Stratonis"</note>, the city Herod named after Augustus, but as Caesarea the capital of Cappadocia, the royal residence formerly called Mazaca (according to the geographer Strabo).

# TALE OF TAJ AL-MULUK AND THE PRINCESS DUNYA:

## *THE LOVER AND THE LOVED.*

There stood in times long gone by, behind the Mountains of Isfahan, a city called the Green City, where a King named Sulayman Shah lived. He was a man of liberality and beneficence, of justice and integrity, of generosity and sincerity. Travelers came to him from every country, and his name was famous in all regions and cities. He reigned for many years in great honor and prosperity, except that he had neither wives nor

When the Minister came into his presence, the King said to him, “O my <term>Wazir</term><note>Minister or Vizier</note>, my heart is heavy, my patience is exhausted, and my strength fails me, because I have neither wife nor child. This is not the way of Kings who rule over all men, princes and paupers alike; for they rejoice in leaving behind children and successors, which doubles their number and their strength. When the Minister heard these words, tears streamed from his eyes, and he replied, “Far be it from me, O King of the Age, to debate matters that belong to the Compassionate One! Would you have me cast into the fire of the All-powerful King’s wrath and ire? Buy yourself a concubine.” 

The King replied, “Know, O Wazir, that when a sovereign buys a female slave, he knows neither her rank nor her lineage. Thus, he cannot tell if she is of lowly origin, so that he might avoid her, or of noble birth, so that he might be intimate in her companionship. If he has relations with her, perhaps she will conceive by him, and her son will be a hypocrite, a man of wrath, and a shedder of blood. Indeed, such a woman may be compared to salt and marshy soil; if one tills it forever, it yields only worthless growth and shows no endurance. For it may be that her son will be hateful in his Lord’s anger, not doing what He commands or failing to refrain from what He forbids. Therefore, I will never cause this by purchasing a concubine. It is my desire that you ask for the hand of the daughter of some King in marriage—one whose lineage is known and whose loveliness is famous. If you can direct me to some maiden of noble birth and piety among the daughters of Muslim Sovereignty, I will ask for her in marriage and wed her in the presence of witnesses, so that I may gain the favor of the Lord of all Creatures.” 

The Wazir said, “O King, truly God has fulfilled your wish and has granted your desire.” He then added, “Know, O King, it has come to my knowledge that King Zahr Shah<note>original: "Zahr Shah"—meaning "Poison King" in Persian or "Flower-King" in Arabic.</note>, Lord of the White Land, has a daughter of surpassing beauty...”

# Tale of Taj al-Muluk and the Princess Dunya

King Sulayman Shah had dispatched his Vizier <term>Wazir: a high-ranking political advisor or minister</term> as a proxy to finalize the marriage, and King Zahr Shah joyfully acted and officiated on behalf of his daughter. The <term>Qadis: Islamic judges</term> concluded the marriage contract and offered up prayers for the happiness and prosperity of the wedded <term>feres: companions or spouses</term>. Afterward, the Vizier rose and brought the gifts, rarities, and precious items, laying them all before the King. 

Then Zahr Shah occupied himself with the preparation of his daughter's dowry and travel needs. He honorably entertained the Vizier and feasted all his subjects, both great and small. For two months they held a grand festival, leaving out nothing that could rejoice the heart and eye. When all the necessary things for the bride were ready, the King ordered the tents to be carried out, and they pitched camp within sight of the city. There, they packed the bride's belongings into chests and prepared the Greek handmaids and Turkish slave girls, providing the Princess with a great store of precious treasures and costly jewels. 

He also had a litter made for her out of red gold, inlaid with pearls and precious stones, and set apart two mules to carry it. This litter was like a chamber in a palace; within it, she looked like one of the loveliest <term>Houris: beautiful maidens who dwell in Paradise</term>, and the carriage itself seemed like one of the pavilions of Paradise. After they had made bales of the treasures and money and loaded them onto the mules and camels, King Zahr Shah traveled with her for a distance of three <term>parasangs: an ancient unit of distance, roughly 3.5 miles or 5.6 kilometers</term>. He then said farewell to her, the Vizier, and their companions, and returned to his home in happiness and safety. 

Thereupon the Vizier, traveling with the King's daughter, pushed on and continued his journey across the desert—

And Shahrazad noticed the dawn of day and stopped her permitted storytelling.

->Now when it was the **Hundred-and-ninth Night**,<-

She said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the Vizier traveled on with the King's daughter. He continued pushing through the stages of the journey across the desert and hastened as fast as possible through nights and days, until only a three-day journey remained between him and his city. At that point, he sent a messenger ahead to King Sulayman Shah to announce the arrival of the bride. The King rejoiced at the news and gave the messenger a robe of honor; he then ordered his troops to march out in a grand procession to meet the Princess.

The place shone with splendor, and the walls glittered with the glamour of its decorations. 

Now when night came, the eunuchs threw open the doors of the bridal chamber and stood surrounding the main entrance. Then the bride came forward; among her maidens, she was like the moon among the stars, or a <term>union: a large, high-quality pearl</term> shining on a string of lesser pearls. She entered the bridal suite, where they had prepared for her a couch of alabaster inlaid with pearls and jewels. As soon as she had taken her seat there, the King came in to her. Allah filled his heart with love for her, so he consummated the marriage, and all his former trouble and anxiety left him. 

He stayed with her for nearly a month, but she had conceived a child by him on the first night. When the month was ended, he went out and sat on his throne of state to dispense justice to his subjects until the months of her pregnancy were finished. On the last day of the ninth month, toward daybreak, the Queen was seized with the pangs of labor. She sat down on the birth stool, and Allah made the labor easy for her. She gave birth to a boy, who showed signs of a fortunate future. When the King heard of this, he rejoiced with exceeding joy and rewarded the messenger who brought the good news with much treasure. In his gladness, he went to the child and kissed him between the eyes, marvelling at his brilliant beauty; for in him the saying of the poet was proven:—

Now, having developed such beauty, when he reached manhood his loveliness only increased, and it won him many friends and companions. Everyone who came near him hoped that Taj al-Muluk Kharan would become Sultan after his father’s death, and that they themselves might become one of his high-ranking officials <term>Emirs</term>. Then he took passionately to chasing and hunting, which he would hardly leave for a single hour. His father, King Sulayman Shah, tried to forbid the pursuit, fearing the dangers of the wilderness and wild beasts for him; however, Taj paid no attention to his warnings.

It happened once that he told his attendants, "Take ten days' worth of food and forage." When they obeyed his bidding, he set out with his entourage for sport and recreation. They rode into the desert and continued riding for four days until they reached a place where the ground was green; there they saw wild beasts grazing, trees with ripe fruit growing, and flowing springs. Taj al-Muluk said to his followers, "Set up the nets here and stake them in a wide ring, and let our meeting place be at the opening of the fence in this spot." 

So they obeyed his words and marked out a wide circle with hunting nets <term>toils</term>. A great many different kinds of wild beasts and gazelles gathered there; they cried out in fear of the men and threw themselves in terror before the horses. When Taj al-Muluk saw them, he said to one of his companions, "Bring me news of those men and ask them why they have stopped in this place." <note>It was considered disrespectful to set up camp close enough to a ruler's camp that their dogs' barking could be heard.</note> So the messenger went up to them and addressed them, "Tell me who you are, and give me an answer without delay."

### Now when the One Hundred and Eleventh Night arrived,

### THE TALE OF AZIZ AND AZIZAH <gloss>3</gloss>

"My father was a wealthy merchant, and <term>Allah</term> [God] had granted him no other child but me. But I had a cousin named Azizah, the daughter of my paternal uncle. The two of us were brought up in one house, for her father was dead, and before his death, he had—"

---

<gloss>1</gloss> Arabic: "Kasabat," meaning "reeds"; here it refers to long, tube-shaped beads or bugles.
<gloss>2</gloss> <note>original: "Koran, xcvi. 5."</note> Quran, 96:5.
<gloss>3</gloss> Both words (masculine and feminine) mean "dear, excellent, or highly prized." This tale is the Arabic version of the European "Patient Griselda" and shows a higher concept of womanly devotion. This is because Azizah, despite her constant weeping, is a highly intelligent girl, while Aziz is a wicked fool—weak as water and as unpredictable as the wind. This phenomenon (which is not rare in real life) is explained by the couplet:
->I love my love with an S—<-
->Because he is stupid and not intellectual.<-
This deep affection that clever women feel for fools can only be explained by the law of opposites, which mostly governs sexual unions in physical matters. Its appearance in this story gives it novelty and purpose. Aziz can only plead the intensity of his passion, which set him apart as a lover from the common crowd of men who cannot love anything beyond themselves. And no one can pity him for losing a member <note>this refers to his later castration</note> that he so greatly abused.

...agreed with my father that I should marry her. So when I reached adulthood and she reached womanhood, they did not separate her from me or me from her, until at last my father spoke to my mother and said, "This very year we will draw up the marriage contract between Aziz and Azizah." Having agreed upon this, he set about preparing the supplies for the wedding feast. We still continued to sleep on the same carpet, knowing nothing of the matter, though she was more thoughtful, more intelligent, and quicker-witted than I. 

Now, when my father had finished his preparations, and nothing remained for him to do but to sign the contract and for me to fulfill the marriage with my cousin, he scheduled the wedding for a certain Friday, after the afternoon prayers. He visited his close friends among the merchants and others to inform them, while my mother went out and invited her female friends and summoned her relatives and family. 

When Friday came, they cleaned the reception room and prepared for the guests, washing the marble floor. Then they spread rugs throughout our house and set out everything that was needed, after they had hung the walls with cloth of gold. The people had agreed to come to our home after the Friday prayers; so my father went out and ordered them to make sweetmeats and sugared dishes, and there remained nothing to do but to sign the contract. 

Then my mother sent me to the <term>Hammam</term> [bathhouse] and sent after me a suit of the richest new clothes. When I came out of the bath, I put on those garments, which were so heavily perfumed that as I walked along, a delicious fragrance drifted from them, scenting the road. I had intended to head to the <term>Great Mosque</term>, when I remembered one of my friends and went back to look for him so that he could be present at the signing of the contract. I said to myself, "This will keep me busy until nearly the time for congregational prayer." 

So I went on and entered a side street which I had never entered before. I was sweating heavily from the effects of the bath and the new clothes on my body, and the sweat streamed down while the scent of my dress was wafted about. I therefore sat down at the upper end of the street, resting on a stone bench after spreading an embroidered handkerchief I had with me underneath myself. The heat oppressed me more and more, making my forehead perspire until the drops trickled down my cheeks; but I could not wipe my face with my handkerchief because it was spread out under me. ### Now when the One Hundred and Thirteenth Night arrived,

She said: It has reached me, O fortunate King, that the youth continued to tell Taj al-Muluk:

So I raised my head to see where this handkerchief had fallen from, and my eyes met those of the lady who owned these gazelles. And behold! She was looking out of a small window in a brass lattice, and my eyes never saw anyone more beautiful than her; in short, my tongue fails to describe her beauty. When she saw me looking at her, she put her index finger in her mouth, then joined her middle finger and her index finger¹ and laid them on her chest, between her breasts. After that, she pulled back her head, closed the window-shutter, and went her way. 

Then a fire broke out in my heart and my pain grew even greater. That one look cost me a thousand sighs, and I remained confused because I heard no word spoken by her, nor did I understand the meaning of her gesture. I looked at the window a second time but found it shut. I waited patiently until sunset, but heard no sound and saw no one. So when I despaired of seeing her again, I stood up and, taking the handkerchief, opened it. A scent of musk wafted from it, giving me such great delight that I felt as if I were in Paradise.² Then I spread it before me, and out dropped a delicate little scroll. I opened the paper, which was perfumed with a delicious fragrance, and in it were written these couplets:

> I sent him a scroll that bore my complaint of love,
> Written in a fine, delicate hand; for writing proves a person's skill.
> Then my friend said to me, “Why is your writing like this?
> It is so fine and thin that it is difficult to read.”
> I said, “Because I am worn down, wasted, and grown thin;
> This is how a lover’s writing should be, for that is how Love wills it.”

<note>1. Edward Lane (i. 608) provides an extensive note on the language of signs, referencing M. du Vigneau’s "The Turkish Secretary" (Paris, 1688), Baron von Hammer-Purgstall (“Mines of the Orient,” No. I, Vienna, 1809) and Marcel’s “Tales of Sheikh El-Mohdy” (Paris, 1833). This practice is common in Africa as well as Asia. In Abeokuta, Yoruba, a person might send a symbolic letter using cowrie shells, palm nuts, and other kernels strung on rice straw, which those with sharp wits can easily interpret. An example is found on page 262 of Miss Tucker’s “Abbeokuta; or Sunrise within the Tropics.”</note>

<note>2. Mr. Payne (ii. 227) translates “Hawá al-’Uzrí” as “the love of the Bani Udhra, an Arabian tribe famous for the passion and devotion with which they practiced love.” See Night 683. I interpret it as “excusable love,” which is translated here as “platonic” for lack of a better term. However, it is more similar to the old custom of “bundling” found in Wales and Northern England; it permits all forms of affection except the final act, similar to what the French call "the pleasures of the little goose" (*les plaisirs de la petite oie*), a term my friend Fred Hankey derived from "the little path" (*la petite voie*). The Afghans call it “Námzad-bází” or betrothed-play (see Burton's *Pilgrimage*, ii. 56); the Abyssinians call it "eye-love"; and the Kaffirs call it *Slambuka* or *Shlabonka*, as described by the traveler Delegorgue.</note>

<note>3. “Turk” in Arabic and Persian poetry refers to a plunderer or a robber. For example, the poet Hafiz wrote: "If that Shirazi (ah, that plunderer!) would deign to take my heart in hand," etc.</note>

<note>4. Arabic “Názir,” meaning a steward or an eye (a “looker”). This poetic wordplay is borrowed from Al-Hariri (Assemblies, xiii).</note>

<note>5. Arabic “Hájib,” meaning a groom of the chambers or a chamberlain; it also means an eyebrow. See Al-Hariri, ibid. xiii. and xxii.</note>

<sup>1</sup> This gesture speaks for itself: it is that of a dyer staining a cloth. The "dyer's" <note>original: "Sabbágh's"</note> shop is the usual small alcove, open to the street, showing pans of various dyes sunk like basins in the floor.
<sup>2</sup> The Arabic *Sabt* <note>original: "Sabt (from sabata, he kept Sabt)"</note> and the Hebrew "Sabbath" both mean Saturn's day, Saturday, transferred by some unknown process throughout the Christian world to Sunday. The change is one of the most curious in the history of religions. If there is a single command stronger than all others, it is "Keep the Saturday holy." It was kept so by the Founder of Christianity; the order was never repealed, and yet most Christians are not aware that Sabbath (or "Sawbath") means Saturn's day, the "Shiyar" <note>original: "Shiyár"</note> of the ancient Arabs. And to complete its degradation, *Sabbat* in French and German means an uproar <note>original: "criailerie"</note>, a "row," a disorder, or an abominable festival of witches <note>original: "Hexen"</note>. This monstrous absurdity can be explained only by the distortions of sectarian zeal and religious party spirit.

She continued to comfort me, but my grief and anxiety only grew. Then she brought me food, which I kicked away so that the contents of every dish were scattered in all directions. I said, "Every lover is a madman; he has no appetite for food, nor does he enjoy sleep." 

My cousin Azizah replied, "By God, my cousin, these are indeed the very signs of love!" Tears streamed down her cheeks as she gathered the broken pieces of the dishes and wiped up the food. Then she sat down and talked to me, while I prayed to God to hurry the dawn.

At last, when morning rose with its bright light, I went out to seek her. Hastening to her side street, I sat down on that bench. Suddenly, the small gate <note>original: "wicket"</note> opened and she poked her head out, laughing. Then she disappeared inside and returned with a mirror, a bag, and a pot full of green plants; she also held a lamp in her hand. The first thing she did was take the mirror, put it in the bag, tie it shut, and throw it back into the room. Then she let her hair fall over her face and set the lamp on the pot of flowers for just a moment. Finally, she gathered everything up and went away, shutting the window without saying a word.

My heart was torn by this turn of events, her secret signals, her mysterious riddles, and her complete silence. Because of this, my longing became more intense, and my passion and confusion doubled. I retraced my steps with tears in my eyes and a heavy heart, returning home to find my cousin sitting with her face to the wall. Her heart was burning with grief and bitter jealousy, yet her love for me prevented her from telling me how much she suffered from passion and longing when she saw the intensity of my own obsession and distraction. 

I looked at her and saw two bandages on her head: one for the injury to her forehead and another over her eye because of the pain she suffered from weeping so much. She was in a miserable state, shedding tears and reciting these verses:

> I count the nights; indeed, I count one night after another; 
> Yet I lived long before I learned to keep such a painful tally.
> Dear friend, I do not understand what God <note>original: "Allah"</note> has willed 
> For Layla, nor what God has destined for me.
> By giving her to another and giving her love to me— 
> What loss but the loss of Layla would I ever have to endure? <note>original: "dree"</note>

I told her everything that had happened, and she said, "Be patient, for the time of your union has come and you have reached the goal of your hopes. As for her signal with the mirror that she put in the bag, it was telling you: 'When the sun has set.' The way she let her hair fall over her face meant: 'When night is near and lets fall its darkness...'"

### *The Tale of Aziz and Azizah*

I found the place exactly as my cousin had described to me and saw the truth of her interpretation of my beloved’s signs. My mind was set at ease, and I felt the pangs of hunger; moreover, the aroma of the food on the table tempted me to eat. Making sure that I would achieve my goal and being famished, I went up to the table, raised the cover, and found in the middle a porcelain dish containing four chickens roasted to a golden red and seasoned with spices. Around the dish were four saucers: one containing sweetmeats, another a preserve of pomegranate seeds, a third almond pastry¹, and a fourth honey-soaked fritters. The contents of these saucers were a mix of sweet and sour. So, I ate some of the fritters and a piece of meat, then moved on to the almond cakes and ate what I could. After that, I fell upon the sweetmeats, swallowing three or four spoonfuls, and finished with part of a chicken and a mouthful of something else.

At this, my stomach became full and my limbs felt loose; I grew too drowsy to stay awake. After washing my hands, I laid my head on a cushion, and sleep overcame me. I did not know what happened to me after this, and I did not wake up until the heat of the sun scorched me, for I had not slept for many days. When I awoke, I found a piece of salt and a bit of charcoal on my stomach. <note>These items are symbolic messages: the charcoal implies "may your face be blackened" (a curse of shame for sleeping), and the salt implies "you are as tasteless as unsalted food" or "may you be preserved."</note> I stood up and shook my clothes, looking right and left, but I could see no one. I discovered that I had been sleeping on the marble pavement without any bedding beneath me. I was perplexed and deeply distressed by this; tears ran down my cheeks, and I mourned my situation. Then I returned home, and when I entered, I found my cousin beating her breast and weeping tears like rain-filled clouds. She recited these verses:

->A cool, sweet breeze blows from my lover’s land, ∘ And with every breath, it makes old love glow anew.<-
->O morning breeze, come show us ∘ That every lover has their fate, their share of joy and woe.<-
->If I could only win my one dearest wish, we would have embraced ∘ With the kind of embrace and closeness that fond lovers know.<-
->God <note>original: "Allah"</note> forbids, while my cousin’s face remains unseen, ∘ All the joys the world can give or the hand of time bestow.<-
->If only Heaven knew if his heart were like mine, ∘ Melted by passion’s flame and filled with a burning fire <term>lowe</term>.<-

When she saw me, she rose in haste, wiped away her tears, and spoke to me softly, saying, "O my cousin, truly God has been gracious to you in your love, because the woman you love loves you in return. I told her everything that had passed, and she smiled reproachfully again and said, "Truly, my heart is full of pain; but may anyone who would hurt your heart not live long! It is as if she were saying to you: 'You need to be salted so that the stomach does not reject you.' You claim to be one of the noble and true lovers, but sleep is forbidden and inappropriate for a lover; therefore, your love is nothing but a lie. 

However, it is actually her love for you that is a lie; for she saw you asleep but did not wake you. If her love for you were true, she would certainly have woken you up. As for the charcoal, it means 'May God blacken your face,'<note>² The curse is full of meaning. On Judgment Day, the righteous shall arise with their faces shining gloriously; hence the blessing, 'May God whiten your countenance!' (original: *Bayyaz’ Allaho wajh-ak*). But the wicked shall appear with faces scorched black and deformed by horror (Koran, chapter 24): hence 'God blacken your brow!' I may observe that Easterners curse, as cursing is the language of intense anger everywhere; but only Westerners, and specifically the English, swear—a practice that is utterly meaningless. 'Damn it,' without specifying what 'it' is, sounds like the speech of a naughty child anxious only to use a 'wicked word.' 'Damn you!' is intelligible all over the world. It has given rise to the nickname '*les goddams*' in France; 'Godámes' in Brazil; and 'Gotáma' among the Somali of Eastern Africa, who learn it in Aden.</note> because you are making a false pretense of love, whereas you are nothing but a child and have no purpose in life other than eating, drinking, and sleeping! Such is the interpretation of her signs, and may God Almighty deliver you from her!" 

When I heard my cousin’s words, I struck my chest and cried out, "By God, this is the absolute truth! I slept, and true lovers do not sleep! Indeed, I have sinned against myself; what could have caused me more harm than eating and—"

### Now when it was the Hundred-and-seventeenth Night,

Then she had me drink jujube-sherbet<note>1. Probably fermented into a kind of wine. This bland fruit (*Unnáb*), which looks like a miniature apple, is used frequently in stews and similar dishes. It is the fruit (known as *Nabak* or classically as *Nabik*) of the *Rhamnus Nabeca* (or *Sidr* tree), also called the *Zizyphus Jujuba*, or <note>original: "seu Spina Christi"</note> *Spina Christi* (the Thorn of Christ), so named because it is fabled to have formed the crown of thorns. This is specifically the use of the "**Ber**" in India, where the leaves are superstitiously held to be particularly pure. Our dictionaries translate "*Sidr*" as "**Lote-tree**"; it is no wonder that those who believe in Homeric writings feel their tempers rise at such a poor representation of that glorious myth. The followers of Homer likely referred to **Hashish** or **Bhang**.</note> and sugar, washed my hands, and dried them with a handkerchief. That night seemed as long to me as if it were a year, but I remained awake until three-quarters of the night were over and the roosters crowed. ### Now when the One Hundred and Nineteenth Night arrived,

She said: I have heard, O fortunate King, that the young merchant continued his story to Taj al-Muluk:

When I was about to leave, she stopped me and said, “Stay until I tell you something and give you a task.” So I stayed while she unfolded a handkerchief, drew out this piece of linen, and spread it open before me. I found the figures of two gazelles embroidered on it and admired it immensely. Then I took the piece of linen and left, feeling joyful, after we had agreed that I should visit her every night in the garden. But in my happiness, I forgot to repeat the verse my cousin had taught me. When she gave me the linen with the gazelles, she had said, “Keep this carefully, for it is my sister’s handiwork.” I asked her, “What is your sister’s name?” and she answered, “Her name is Nur al-Huda.” 

When I returned to my cousin, I found her lying down. As soon as she saw me, she stood up with tears streaming from her eyes. She came to me, kissed my chest, and asked, “Did you do as I instructed? Did you repeat the verse to her?” 

“I forgot it,” I replied; “nothing drove it from my mind except these two embroidered gazelles.” 

I threw the piece of linen on the floor in front of her. She stood up and sat down again, unable to contain her restlessness, and her eyes overflowed with tears as she recited these two couplets:

> O you who seek to leave, go gently! Do not let the beautiful woman deceive you with her clever arts.
> Go gently, for it is the nature of Fate to trick us, and the end of every meeting is a parting.

When she finished her recitation, she said, “O my cousin, give me this piece of linen.” I gave it to her, and she took it and unfolded it to see what was there. When the appointed time came for me to go to my lover, my uncle’s daughter said to me, “Go, and may peace go with you. But when you are about to leave her, recite the verse I taught you long ago, which you forgot.”

¹ I have explained "Nu'umán's flower" as the anemone which in Latinized Arabic is "Anúmiyá." Here they are scattered over the tomb; often the flowers are planted in a small bed of soil set into the top surface.

² Arabic "Barzakh," literally a bar or a partition: in the Quran (chapters 23 and 35), it is the space or place between death and resurrection where souls are kept. It corresponds in a way to the classical Hades and the Limbo <note>original: "Limbus"</note> of Christianity—for example, the Limbo of the Fathers, of infants, or of the foolish <note>original: "Limbus patrum, infantum, fatuorum"</note>. ³ Arabic "Zukák al-Nakíb"; the latter word has been explained as a chief, leader, or head man.

<sup>1</sup> Muslims never stand up at such times, for a spray of urine would make their clothes ceremonially impure; therefore, the scrupulous will break up the hard ground in front of them with a stick or knife. A certain pilgrim was reported to have made this blunder, which is hardly possible in Muslim dress. A high-ranking person once asked me if it was true that he killed a man who caught him in a standing position; and I found to my surprise that this absurd rumor was already twenty years old. After urinating, the Muslim wipes the tip of the penis <note>original: "os penis"</note> with one to three bits of stone, clay, or handfuls of earth, and he must perform ritual ablution <term>Wudu</term> before he can pray. Tournefort (*Voyage au Levant* iii. 335) tells a pleasant story of certain Christians at Constantinople who powdered the stones in a wall where the Muslims were in the habit of rubbing the tip of the penis with cayenne pepper <note>original: "Poivre-d’Inde"</note> as a way of wiping. The same author (ii. 336) strongly recommends a translation of Rabelais’ "bum-wiping" <note>original: "Torcheculative"</note> chapter (Book i., chapter 13) for the benefit of Mohammedans.

I asked, "What is the history of this letter?", and she replied, "O my son, this letter is from my son, who has been absent for a term of ten years. He has a sister who weeps for him night and day; I told her, 'He is well and all right,' but she will not believe me. I will call his sister to listen from inside the door, and in this way you shall dispel our anxiety and fulfill our need. Truly, the <term>Messenger of Allah</term> <note>original: "Apostle of Allah"</note> (whom Allah bless and preserve!) said: 'Whoever relieves a troubled person of one of the troubles of this difficult world, Allah will relieve him of a hundred troubles'; and according to another tradition: 'Whoever relieves his brother of one of the troubles of this difficult world, Allah shall relieve him of seventy-two troubles on the Day of Resurrection.' And so I have come to you; do not disappoint me." I replied, "To hear is to obey; go on ahead of me!"

So she walked on, leading the way, and I followed her a little distance until she came to the gate of a large and handsome mansion whose door was plated with copper. <margin>Arabic: "Nuhás ahmar," literally red brass.</margin> I stood behind the door while the old woman cried out in Persian, and before I knew it, a young woman ran up with a light and nimble step. She had tucked up her trousers to her knees, so that I saw a pair of calves that would astound anyone who thought of them or saw them. The girl herself was just as the poet described her:

> O you who show your leg's calf, it is better only to suggest * To the passion-mad lover that better things lie above!
> Toward its lover the bowl goes round and runs; * The cup <note>The cup is a metaphor for the lady's private parts.</note> and the cup-bearer only drive us mad with love. <note>A play upon "Sak" (calf/leg) and "Saki" (cup-bearer). The "going round" (Tawaf) and "running" (Sa'i) refer to the religious rituals of the Kaaba and the run between Mount Safa and Marwah. A religious Muslim would find this comparison highly irreverent.</note>

Now these legs were like two pillars of alabaster adorned with gold anklets, which were set with precious stones. Her ears were adorned with pearl pendants, and on her head she wore a brand-new brocade kerchief <note>Lane (vol. 1, p. 614) never saw a woman wearing such a kerchief, which is considered casual dress. She had tucked the skirt of her chemise into the drawstring of her trousers, as she was busy with household chores. Then she spoke with soft, refined speech—I have never heard anything sweeter—"O my mother! Is this the man who has come to read the letter?" 

"It is," replied the old woman, and she reached out her hand toward me with the letter. Now, between her and the door was a distance of about half a rod <note>The "Kasabah" was a unit of measurement of about twelve feet, though the length has varied over time.</note>; so I stretched out my hand to take the letter from her, leaning my head and shoulders inside the door so I could get closer and read it. Before I realized what she was planning, the old woman rammed her head into my back and pushed me forward with the letter in my hand. Before I could think, I found myself in the middle of the hall, far past the entryway. Then she entered faster than a flash of blinding lightning and did nothing but shut the door.

Finally, we came to a great hall with four raised platforms, which was so large that a horseman could have played polo inside. <note>“Bat and ball,” or hockey on horseback (Polo), is one of the earliest Persian games, as shown by every illustrated copy of Firdausi’s *Shahnámeh*. This game was played with a *Kurrah* (a small hand-ball) and a long, thin bat crooked at the end, called *Chaugán* in Persian and *Saulaján* in Arabic. Another meaning of the word is found in the *Burhán-i-Káti* (translated by Vullers in his Persian-Latin Dictionary): a large staff with a bent head from which an iron ball is hung, also called a *Kaukabah* (our “morning star” mace); like the umbrella, it symbolizes the high officials of the court. A similar *Kaukabah* was a notable distinction of one of the Marquesses of Waterford. This polo corresponds with the *folliculus*, the *pallone*, or the “ball-game” of medieval Europe, where the horse was not as constant a companion to man, and of which the classics sang: 

->*It is fitting for boys to play with the ball, and for old men as well.* <note>original: "Folle decet pueros ludere, folle senes."</note><-

In these days, we might interpret the “folly” of seniors playing at ball or lawn tennis differently.</note> Here she released me, saying, “Open your eyes.”

So I opened them, still dizzy from her intense embracing and squeezing, and saw that the entire hall was built of the finest marbles and alabasters. All its furniture was made of silk and brocade, even down to the cushions and mattresses. Inside, there were also two benches of yellow brass and a couch of red gold, set with pearls and precious stones, suitable for no one except kings like yourself. Off the main hall were smaller sitting rooms, and the whole place was redolent of wealth.

Then she asked, “O Aziz, which is more desirable to you: life or death?”

“Life,” I answered. 

She said, “If life is more desirable to you, then marry me.” 

I replied, “Indeed, I would hate to marry someone like you.” 

She said, “If you marry me, you will at least be safe from the daughter of Dalilah the Wily One.” <note><term>Dalil</term> means a guide; <term>Dalilah</term> refers to a woman who misleads others, a procuress or "bawd." See the Tale of Dalilah the Crafty, Night 698.</note> 

I asked, “And who is this daughter of the Wily One?” 

At this, she laughed and replied, “It is she who has lived with you this day for a year and four months—may the Almighty destroy her and afflict her with someone worse than herself! By Allah, there lives no one more treacherous than she. How many men has she slain before you, and what deeds has she done! I cannot understand how you have been in her company all this time, yet she has not killed you or done you any harm.” 

When I heard her words, I wondered with great amazement and said, “O my lady, who told you about her?”
